bounce.strip: Every strike of the two balls on a time line

play.title: Let them fall
play.hint: Both balls hang over the plate. Let them go and listen: with the sound on, every strike clicks. Below, every strike on a time line.
play.sound_hint: A click at every strike, as loud as the strike. Silent until you turn it on.
play.no_sound: Your browser cannot make sound here.
play.waiting: The balls hang over the plate, waiting.
play.caption: The balls at true size over the plate, from {{height}} cm; below, every strike on the time line, until both lie still.

change.title: A ball of your own
change.hint: Choose a ball, change its restitution and the height it falls from. The height applies to the two balls above too.
change.restitution_hint: The share of its speed a strike gives back.
change.height_hint: How high over the plate the ball is let go.
change.status: Your ball lies still after {{time}} s; {{count}} of its bounces last longer than a hundredth of a second.

chart.still_hint: How long the two balls bounce, by their restitution, from the height set; dashed, without air. Near 1 the time grows without bound.

model.intro: At every strike the ball loses a fixed share of its speed: it and the plate give a little, and motion turns into heat and sound. What is left, the restitution says.
model.bounce: A strike gives back the share e of the speed; so the ball rises to e² of the height before.
model.series: Without air every bounce lasts e times as long as the one before.
model.sum: All the bounces' times together are a geometric series: infinitely many terms, but a finite sum.
model.air: The air brakes with the square of the speed. For the heavy steel ball that is almost nothing, for the light table-tennis ball it shows.

symbols.still: time until the ball lies still
symbols.t0: time of the fall to the first strike

sweet.zeno: The trick: the bounces grow not only lower but shorter too, each by the same share. So infinitely many bounces fit into a finite time, as in Zeno's riddle of Achilles and the tortoise.
sweet.steel: From 30 cm the steel ball, restitution 0.95, lies still after 9.6 s, with 75 bounces that last longer than a hundredth of a second; the table-tennis ball, 0.92, after 5.2 s, with 44. The small difference in restitution counts for a lot, as the time grows with 1/(1 − e).
sweet.rhythm: You can hear the restitution in the rhythm: the steel ball's second bounce lasts 0.95 times as long as its first, its restitution exactly. For the table-tennis ball it is 0.89 rather than 0.92, as the air brakes it too, the air that carries it whole at 8.6 m/s; the steel ball only at 60 m/s.
sweet.rules: The rules of table tennis demand that a ball dropped from 305 mm onto a steel block bounce back to between 240 and 265 mm. With a restitution of 0.92 and the air, this one bounces to 240 mm, at the lower limit.

computed.system: Between two strikes the ball flies straight up and down, with only its weight and the air's drag. That has an exact solution, upward with the tangent, downward with the hyperbolic tangent. The page computes flight after flight; once the flights are shorter than a tenth of a millisecond, the rest of the series is added in closed form, the air long negligible there.
computed.exact: Thrown up at v₀: the speed and the height of the top; coming down, the speed a time t into the fall.
computed.check: The page's tests hold every flight to the equation of motion with air, stepped through (Runge–Kutta), and the sum for a ball the air hardly touches to the geometric series √(2h/g)·(1 + e)/(1 − e). The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: that the restitution depends on the speed (here it is fixed); the time the ball spends on the plate at each strike, less than a ten-thousandth of a second, which in reality ends the series with a buzz before its sum; spin; the plate giving way. The values: a steel ball of 20 mm (33 g) with a restitution of 0.95 on hardened steel, an assumption; a regulation table-tennis ball (2.7 g, 40 mm) with 0.92.

at.blocks: Nine identical wooden blocks lie ready, and the edge of a table. No glue, no nails: how far does the top block reach out over the edge?
at.most: Most people build a staircase in even steps and do not quite reach one block's length.
at.further: Yet four blocks, shifted right, already reach more than a whole length out, and nine a length and two fifths.

overhang.view: The table's edge with the stack; the blocks can be dragged or moved with the arrow keys

play.title: Stack them
play.hint: Drag the blocks right or left, or pick one with the Tab key and move it with the arrow keys, in big steps with Shift. The dots are centres of mass: green where the stack holds, red where it tips.
play.count_hint: How many blocks the stack has.
play.caption: Blocks of {{length}} × {{height}} cm, schematic from the front, the table's edge dashed. Each dot is the centre of mass of a block and all above it, where it rests on the block below.
play.holds: The stack holds. It reaches {{cm}} cm out over the edge, {{lengths}} block lengths.
play.tips_one: The stack tips: the top block's centre of mass lies beside the block below.
play.tips_other: The stack tips: the centre of mass of the top {{count}} blocks lies beside their footing.

model.intro: A block stays put as long as its centre of mass lies over the block below – the centre of mass of it and of everything on it. All lengths are in block lengths L.
model.holds: The stack holds if at every layer the centre of mass of all the blocks from it upward lies over its footing: over the stretch where it touches the block below, for the lowest over the table.
model.step: Built from the top, each block as far out as the ones above allow: the k-th block from the top juts 1/(2k) out over the next.
model.harmonic: Together that is half the harmonic series.
model.even: In even steps, the bottom block jutting over the table as far as each block over the one below, the whole stack's centre of mass reaches the edge first: n blocks reach n/(n + 1) out, never a whole length.

symbols.centre: centre of mass of the blocks from layer k up
symbols.d: how far the k-th block from the top juts over the next

sweet.steps: The trick: build from the top, not from the bottom. The top block may jut half a length out, the top two together a quarter over the third, the top three a sixth: the steps grow smaller downward. Nine blocks then reach 1.41 lengths out, 28 cm with blocks of 20 cm; in even steps only 0.9, and 0.94 with the bottom block set back a little: never a whole length.
sweet.endless: The harmonic series has no end: with enough blocks the stack reaches as far out as you like. But slowly, like a logarithm. This many blocks it takes:
sweet.knife: A stack built so stands on a knife's edge: every layer lies exactly at the end of its footing. One block a breath further out and the whole stack tips over the table's edge. A real one is therefore built a little short.

chart.hint: How far a stack can reach out at most, by the number of blocks: shifted furthest and in even steps.

computed.system: The page checks at every layer whether the centre of mass of the blocks from it upward lies over its footing; a stack of one block a layer needs nothing more. The furthest stack is built from the top, each block 1/(2k) further out.
computed.check: The page's tests work the overhang out again in exact fractions and search blindly among twenty thousand random stacks of three and of four blocks each: none that holds reaches further than the harmonic one. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: stacks with several blocks to a layer, some of them counterweights – which reach further still (Paterson and Zwick); friction, as the blocks here never slide, they only tip; the wood giving way; a shaking hand. The blocks are 20 cm long and 4 cm high.

at.bottle: In a bottle full of water floats a small glass tube, open at the bottom, with a bubble of air at its top that just keeps it afloat.
at.squeeze: Squeeze the bottle and the diver sinks; let go and it rises again.
at.hover: In between there is a depth where it would hover. But it never stays there: it sinks on or it rises.

diver.view: The bottle with its water, the diver and the depth it would hover at

play.title: Squeeze the bottle
play.hint: Squeeze the bottle with the slider. Try to keep the diver hovering in the middle.
play.squeeze_hint: How much the hand raises the pressure in the bottle.
play.caption: The bottle, {{depth}} cm of water; dashed, the depth the diver would hover at with this squeeze. The diver is drawn larger than it is.

motion.floats: The diver floats at the top.
motion.bottom: The diver lies on the bottom.

change.title: Rebuild the diver
change.hint: Give the diver more or less air and change the height of the water.
change.air_hint: The bubble at the surface, unsqueezed. Under 1.81 cm³ it would go under.
change.depth_hint: How deep the water in the bottle is.

figures.sinking: Squeeze that sinks it from the top
figures.bottom: Squeeze under which it rises from the bottom

chart.hover_hint: The depth the diver would hover at, by the hand's squeeze; dashed, the surface and the bottom.
chart.lift_hint: Buoyancy less weight by depth, for three squeezes of the hand. Where a line crosses zero it hovers; above, it rises, below, it sinks.

model.intro: The diver floats because with its glass and its bubble it displaces a little more water than it weighs. The air can be squeezed, the glass cannot.
model.boyle: The bubble shrinks as the pressure grows: the air's pressure, the hand's squeeze and the weight of the water above it (Boyle's law).
model.lift: Buoyancy less weight: it rises while the water it displaces weighs more than it does.
model.hover: The depth where the two are equal. Every kilopascal of the hand's squeeze lifts it by 10.2 cm.
model.motion: The motion: to the glass's mass add the water it drags along, and the water brakes it.

sweet.unstable: The trick: the balance is unstable. A little below the hover depth the water squeezes the bubble harder, the diver grows heavier for its size and sinks on, to the bottom. A little above, the bubble grows and it rises to the surface. Half a centimetre off is enough for it to go all the way.
sweet.numbers: The diver here has 3 g of glass (1.2 cm³) and 2 cm³ of air; at the surface it carries 0.19 g more than it weighs. From a squeeze of 10.9 kPa it sinks from the top; under 7.9 kPa it rises even from the bottom of the 30 cm bottle. To hover it needs a bubble of 1.81 cm³.
sweet.chase: To keep it hovering you must chase it all the time: ease off when it sinks, squeeze when it rises – and more than you think, as the hover depth moves 10 cm with every kilopascal.

computed.system: The page steps the motion every 2 ms (Runge–Kutta), with the hand's squeeze as it is at that moment. At the surface the diver floats; on the bottom it lies.
computed.check: The page's tests hold the bubble to Boyle's law, show the buoyancy vanishing exactly at the hover depth, lifting above it and pulling below, and hold the steps to the same equation stepped twenty times finer. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: that water must first run into the tube before the bubble shrinks (here it follows the pressure at once); the water and the bottle giving a little; the air in the bottle's neck, whose pressure here is the hand's squeeze directly; the diver poking out of the water at the surface; temperature. The values are an assumed diver: 3 g of glass (1.2 cm³) and 2 cm³ of air, in a bottle 30 cm deep.

at.wall: A wall is coated with tiny glass beads, each smaller than a millimetre. A lamp beside your head lights it.
at.ring: Round the shadow of your head a coloured ring glows: red outside, blue inside, and within the ring the wall is brighter than outside it.
at.smaller: It is a rainbow – but only half the size of the one in the sky. And whoever stands next to you sees a different ring, round their own head.

rainbow.wall_view: The wall of glass beads with the coloured ring round the shadow of the head

change.title: Change the material
change.hint: Choose glass or water and change the refractive index.
change.index_hint: How strongly the material bends light, for yellow light. How widely it fans the colours out stays the material's.

figures.impact: Where the rainbow ray meets the bead
figures.near: Of it, in the last degree before the rainbow angle

chart.exit_hint: The angle out against where the ray meets the bead, for violet and red light. Where the curve is flat at its top, many rays come back at almost the same angle: the ring.
chart.angle_hint: The rainbow angle against the refractive index.

model.intro: A ray of light enters the bead, is reflected once at its back and leaves again – back towards the lamp, but off by an angle.
model.snell: Going in and coming out, the ray is bent (Snell's law).
model.leaves: The angle between the ray leaving and the way back to the lamp. A ray at the bead's centre comes straight back.
model.bow: The largest angle out, the rainbow angle: there θ hardly changes as the ray meets the bead a little further out, and many rays come back together. It depends only on the refractive index.
model.dispersion: Blue light is bent a little more than red (Cauchy). So each colour has its own ring; red's is the largest.

symbols.theta: Angle out, from the way back to the lamp
symbols.ir: Angle of incidence of the rainbow ray
symbols.nd: Refractive index for yellow light (the sodium line)
symbols.b: How widely the colours fan out (Cauchy's coefficient)

sweet.index: The trick: the ring depends only on the material, not on the size of the bead. Water drops send the light back at 42°, glass of index 1.52 at 21° – half as far. That is why the glass-bead ring is half the size of the rainbow in the sky.
sweet.two: The more strongly the material bends light, the smaller the ring. At index 2 it shrinks to nothing: then all the light near the centre comes straight back to where it came from.
sweet.own: Because every bead sends the light back at the same angle, you see the ring in all the beads that lie at that angle from the shadow of your own head – a circle round it. Whoever stands next to you sees a different ring, round their own head.

computed.system: The page follows each ray through the bead by the laws of refraction and reflection. For the picture of the wall it cuts the bead's face into 2000 rings of equal area and spreads each ring's light over the angles it comes back at – less what the surface lets through or reflects (Fresnel). The lamp is as large as the sun in the sky and blurs the ring by as much.
computed.colours: The colours: for 81 wavelengths from 380 to 780 nm, weighted by the eye's sensitivity to colour (CIE 1931) and converted into the screen's colours (sRGB). The lamp's white appears white, as the eye sees it; spectral colours that a screen cannot show appear somewhat paler.
computed.check: The page's tests hold the drawn ray to the law of refraction and to the formula θ = 4r − 2i, search for the rainbow angle blindly across the whole bead, and count the light sent back by Simpson's rule: of the light meeting a glass bead, 5.5 % comes back after one reflection, 24 % of that in the last degree before the rainbow angle. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: the size of the beads (in very small beads the light's waves widen the ring and add faint rings inside it); light reflected twice or more inside (a second, fainter ring, for glass far out of sight) or not at all (the beads' white sheen); the wall behind the beads. Assumed: soda-lime glass of refractive index 1.52.

at.end: Looking in at the other end, the white lamp appears orange – like the sun in the evening.

air.ozone_takes: Of the orange (600 nm), ozone absorbs

model.intro: Particles much smaller than the wavelength scatter light the more strongly, the shorter its wavelength.
model.rayleigh: Scattering grows with the fourth power of the frequency (Rayleigh): blue light (450 nm) is scattered 4.4 times as strongly as red (650 nm).
model.beer: What is scattered is missing from the light going on: it falls exponentially along the tube, blue fastest (Beer–Lambert).
model.side: From the side one sees what is scattered at that place, less what is still lost on the way to the tube's wall.
model.sky: The sky straight overhead: sunlight scattered once at every height and then going down to the ground. The sun stands m air masses low. It reaches the eye turned through 90° less the sun's height, and the air scatters half as much sideways as straight on: with the sun low the sky overhead is half as bright for it.
model.ozone: The ozone layer, some 22 km up, does not scatter light, it absorbs it – most of all orange (600 nm). Straight up its optical depth there is only 0.041, little beside the air's.
model.ozone_mass: Sunlight crosses it as a thin shell: m₃ times as much ozone as straight down, 12 times at the horizon – where it absorbs 39 % of the orange. Since it lies above nearly all the air, the sky's light, scattered further down, carries the same factor.

symbols.beta0: Cloudiness: the scattering coefficient at 550 nm
symbols.i: Light in the tube, as a share of the lamp's
symbols.tau: Optical depth of the air straight up (0.097 at 550 nm)
symbols.m: Air mass: how much air the sunlight crosses, against the way straight down
symbols.t3: What the ozone layer lets through of the sunlight
symbols.sigma: Absorption cross-section of an ozone molecule, measured (Serdyuchenko et al. 2014)
symbols.n: Ozone molecules above each square centimetre of ground: 300 Dobson units
symbols.m3: Ozone air mass: how much ozone the sunlight crosses, against the way straight down
symbols.hh: Height of the ozone layer (22 km)

sweet.same: The trick: the tube is the sky in small. The molecules of the air are much smaller than the wavelength and scatter blue 4.4 times as strongly as red. Wherever one looks away from the sun, one sees scattered light – and it is blue.
sweet.sunset: In the evening the sun stands low, and its light crosses 38 times as much air as light coming straight down. On the way the blue is scattered almost entirely away: only 3 % of the sunlight arrives (4 % without the ozone layer), and it is orange – like the lamp at the end of the tube.
sweet.not_violet: Violet is scattered even more strongly than blue. That the sky still looks blue and not violet is down to the sun, which sends out less violet, and to the eye, which is little sensitive to it – the page's colour computation shows both.
sweet.ozone: And why is the sky overhead still blue at sunset, when the sunlight has lost its blue on the way? What the air scatters down of it would be almost white. But on that long, flat way the ozone layer absorbs mostly orange, and the blue stays. Switch the ozone off above and put the sun on the horizon.

computed.system: For each of 81 wavelengths the page computes how much light is still there at each place of the tube and how much of it is scattered to the side. For the sky it takes the air's optical depth, 0.097 at 550 nm, and the air mass by Kasten and Young, 37.9 at the horizon. For ozone it takes the measured cross-section (Serdyuchenko et al. 2014, averaged over each 5 nm), 300 Dobson units and a thin layer 22 km up.
computed.colours: The colours as for the glass-bead rainbow: weighted by the eye's sensitivity to colour (CIE 1931) and converted into the screen's colours (sRGB). The lamp's white – for the sky, the sun's above the air – appears white. Each colour is drawn as bright as the screen allows for it; how bright it really is, the figures say.
computed.check: The page's tests count that the light scattered to the side and the light arriving at the end add up to exactly the lamp's light (Simpson's rule), and hold the sky overhead against the same sum over all heights. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: light scattered more than once (it makes a very cloudy tube and the sky at the horizon whiter); larger particles, which scatter all colours alike (that is why milk is white); the direction of scattering in the tube, which changes only the brightness; for the sky, dust and haze, which make the sunset redder still, the sun below the horizon (the sky overhead is then lit only high up, through still more ozone), and how much ozone there is, which changes with the season and the place. Assumed: a tube 1 m long and 6 cm across.

model.intro: Light is a wave. From each slit a wave goes to every point of the wall; there the two add up.
model.path: The two waves' difference in path. Is it a whole number of wavelengths, they arrive in step: bright. Is it half a wavelength more, they cancel: dark.
model.intensity: The brightness on the wall (Fraunhofer): each slit alone gives the broad middle band (sin β/β)², the two together the stripes within it (cos² α).
model.stripes: The spacing of the stripes on the wall: the longer the wavelength and the further the wall, the wider; the further apart the slits, the narrower.

sweet.dark: The trick: at the first dark stripe one slit alone gives 97 % of the brightness of its middle. Open the second slit and more light comes – and just there it goes dark. The two waves arrive half a wavelength apart and cancel. Light plus light makes dark.
sweet.colours: With white light each colour has its own stripes, red ones further apart than blue. Only the middle is bright for all of them: it stays white, beside it the stripes turn coloured. Where red cancels, blue still shines.

computed.system: The page computes the brightness at each point of the wall with the formula for a distant wall (Fraunhofer). The laser is red, 650 nm; the slits are 0.25 mm apart and 0.05 mm wide each, the wall 2 m behind them. Then the stripes lie 5.2 mm apart, the first dark one 2.6 mm beside the middle, and 9 bright stripes fit into one slit's middle band, which reaches 26 mm to either side of the middle.
computed.colours: The laser's colour is its wavelength's, as saturated as the screen can show it and as bright as the light is there. White light: for 81 wavelengths each its own pattern, weighted by the eye's sensitivity to colour (CIE 1931) and converted into the screen's colours (sRGB).
computed.check: The page's tests cut each slit into 400 narrow strips, add up the waves of all the strips at each point of the wall (Huygens) and compare the result with the formula. They check that the dark stripes are exactly dark where one slit alone gives light, and that white light is blue where red cancels. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: that the wall is not infinitely far away (the formula holds to a per cent once it is more than thirty-five times a²/λ away, a a slit's width: here 13 cm; nearer, the page says so); the laser beam's width and spread, which make the stripes fade out up and down; the slits' edges and thickness; the light's polarisation.

model.intro: Each fork swings at its frequency and slowly dies away. At your ear the two swings add up.
model.sum: The sum is a tone of the mean frequency whose strength slowly rises and falls: now the forks swing in step, now against each other.
model.beat: The loudness peaks as many times a second as the frequencies differ.
model.rider: The rider slows the prong like an added mass (Rayleigh): hardly at all near the stem, where the prong barely swings, fully at the tip. At its tip the prong acts like a quarter of its mass.

sweet.closer: The trick: the closer the two tones, the slower the beats. Here they are only 0.82 Hz apart, 3.2 cents – and yet one clearly hears a beat every 1.22 s, 23 until it dies away.
sweet.tuning: That is how instruments are tuned: play two tones together and adjust until the beats slow down and finally vanish.
sweet.rider: The rider hardly matters near the stem and fully at the tip: 1 g at 30 % of the prong detunes the fork by 0.82 Hz, at the tip by 38 Hz.

computed.system: The page computes the second fork's frequency by Rayleigh's method from the mode shape of a clamped prong (βL = 1.875) and adds the two dying swings. Assumed: a fork of 440 Hz, prongs of 20 g, a decay time of 6 s.
computed.check: The page's tests hold the mode shape to its equation, check that the prong acts at its tip like a quarter of its mass, and compare Rayleigh's estimate with the exact frequency of a prong with a mass at its tip: for 1 g it is less than 0.1 % high. The computing happens in your browser, with the same formulas as the site's engine.
computed.left_out: Left out: the sounding boxes and the room; that the rider itself changes the mode shape a little; the coupling of the two prongs, and the stem; the ear, which hears fast beats no longer as swelling and fading but as roughness and finally as two tones.
