small_swing.title: A small swing at the bottom
small_swing.setting: Sphere Ø 40 cm, solid ball Ø 4 cm, no rolling resistance, no hand: let go 2° up the wall.
small_swing.reads: Rolling, the ball swings like a pendulum of length ρ under 5/7 of gravity; the other 2/7 spin it.
small_swing.why: Checks the rolling: sliding, the same ball would swing at 1.17 Hz. The 0.008 % off is the 2° swing's own, as the formula is for the smallest.

hollow_ball.title: The hollow ball
hollow_ball.setting: As above, with a thin hollow ball.
hollow_ball.reads: The same formula with k = 2/3: a hollow ball has its mass outside and takes more to spin.
hollow_ball.why: Checks that the moment of inertia enters, not a fixed 5/7.
hollow_ball.step: The first source gives the formula for any k = I/(m r²); put in is the hollow ball's k = 2/3 from the second.

wide_swing.title: A wide swing up to the level
wide_swing.setting: Solid ball, no rolling resistance, let go 90° up the wall.
wide_swing.reads: Swung wide, a pendulum slows, by π/(2K) with the elliptic integral K.
wide_swing.why: Checks the equation of motion far from small angles: 0.84 Hz, not 0.99 Hz. K is summed here as an integral, not by the arithmetic-geometric mean the engine uses.
wide_swing.step: The first source shows the rolling ball obeys the pendulum equation exactly, with g/(1+k); the second gives its period at any amplitude.

circle_any_size.title: A circle, as deep in any sphere
circle_any_size.setting: Sphere Ø 1 m, not 40 cm, solid ball Ø 4 cm, no rolling resistance: started on the circle for 2 Hz and run for 10 s.
circle_any_size.reads: A circle at rate Ω lies g′/Ω² below the equator, whatever the sphere's size.
circle_any_size.why: Checks the motion in space, not in one plane only: after 10 s the ball is still 4.4358 cm down, as in the 40 cm sphere.
circle_any_size.step: For the rolling ball this is a conical pendulum under g′ = g/(1+k). The sources show the spin about the normal is kept (Routh). That the centre then moves as a spherical pendulum under g′ follows in one step none of them writes out.

wobble.title: The wobble of a tilted circle
wobble.setting: Solid ball on the circle at 60°, but started 0.3° too high.
wobble.reads: A slightly disturbed circle bobs at Ω·√(1 + 3cos²θ).
wobble.why: Checks how stable the circle is, which the page calls “not in the plane yet”. 0.3° is not infinitely small, hence 0.02 % off.
wobble.step: The source does the spherical pendulum, with the angle from the downward vertical as here; for the rolling ball under g′ = g/(1+k), as for the circle.

energy.title: Energy is kept
energy.setting: Solid ball started at 60° with 0.3 m/s sideways, no rolling resistance, no hand, for 20 s.
energy.reads: With no losses, motion, spin and height add to the same; the spin carries k times the motion's.
energy.why: Checks the time loop itself: after 20,000 steps the energy is the same to 10⁻¹¹.

grip.title: How much grip rolling needs
grip.setting: Solid ball let go at 60°; read at the turning point.
grip.reads: Rolling without slipping needs a grip of at least tan θ/(1 + m r²/I), (2/7)·tan θ for a solid ball.
grip.why: Checks the friction the page gives: 0.49 at 60°.
grip.step: The source does the incline. At the turning point the ball stands still and lies as on an incline of the same slope.

leaves_wall.title: Where the ball falls off the wall
leaves_wall.setting: Solid ball pushed at the bottom so fast that without the wall it would reach 120°.
leaves_wall.reads: The wall pushes with g·cos θ + 2g′(cos θ − cos θ₀). Where that is zero the ball falls: at cos θ = 2cos θ₀/(3 + k).
leaves_wall.why: Checks the wall's push, by which the page notices the ball falling: at 107.1°.
leaves_wall.step: The source gives the simple pendulum's string tension, mg(3cos θ − 2cos θ_m). For the rolling ball the energy carries the factor 1 + k; the push across the wall is still g·cos θ + v²/ρ.

rl_rise.title: The current rises
rl_rise.setting: Plus held, the car at the top of a ramp, far from the coil; read after four time constants.
rl_rise.reads: Switched onto a voltage, the current in a coil rises only slowly, with the time constant τ = L/R.
rl_rise.why: Checks the page's circuit: 94 mA after 5 ms, 96 mA in the end.

wheeler.title: The coil's inductance
wheeler.setting: 1600 turns, 60 mm mean diameter, 50 mm long.
wheeler.reads: Wheeler's formula of 1928, in inches and microhenries, good to 1 %.
wheeler.why: Checks the inductance: the page's 118.1 mH is the SI form of the same formula, Wheeler as printed gives 117.8 mH. The 0.28 % lie within his own per cent, as his 9 and 10 are rounded.

flux_centre.title: The magnet's flux through the coil
flux_centre.setting: The magnet, Ø 20 × 10 mm and 1.3 T, in the middle of the coil.
flux_centre.reads: Each turn holds a share of the small magnet's flux; summed turn by turn over all 1600.
flux_centre.why: Checks the curve Ψ(x) both the voltage and the force come from: the sum over the turns meets the page's closed form to 10⁻⁷.
flux_centre.step: The first source gives a loop's field on its axis, the second that mutual inductance is the same both ways: the magnet's flux through the loop is its moment times that field per ampere. The third writes the same for a coil.

charge.title: The charge, the same at any speed
charge.setting: No buttons, no rolling resistance, let go from halfway up a ramp; counted to the coil's middle.
charge.reads: Through the meter flows the change of flux over the resistance, however fast the car goes.
charge.why: Checks Faraday's law on the time loop: 888 µC. The 0.1 % off: the coil still holds L·i/R back at the middle, and the page draws 200 times a second.
charge.step: The source gives a search coil's charge without inductance. With it the same holds once the current is zero at start and end; at the middle it nearly is.

period.title: Without the coil: a swing on arcs
period.setting: Coil open, no rolling resistance, let go from halfway up a ramp; the time there and back.
period.reads: On each arc the car swings half a period like a pendulum of length R; between them it crosses the flat twice at the speed of its drop.
period.why: Checks the track and the time loop: 2.71554 s to five places.
period.step: The first source gives the motion on a circular arc, with β = 0 for a body that slides rather than rolls; the second its period at any amplitude.

brake.title: The coil's brake
brake.setting: A car a hundred times heavier, 15 kg, so it hardly slows; coil closed, no rolling resistance, let go from halfway up a ramp. Measured to its first turn on the right.
brake.reads: The induced voltage k·v drives a current that brakes with k²v²/R; over one pass (1/R)·∫k²v dx, with the speed v from the drop alone.
brake.why: Checks Lenz's brake, which stops the coasting car sooner: 1.10 mJ on the way through the coil, measured as the height the heavy car falls short on the other side.
brake.step: The sources give a magnet's drag in a coil and a moving conductor's power; summed along the way, with the speed from the energy, they give one pass's loss.

energy_account.title: The energy account closes
energy_account.setting: Ten seconds pressing by the rule: plus coming in, minus going out.
energy_account.reads: What the battery gives becomes heat in the wire, rolling loss, sparks on letting go, the knock at the end stop, the car's motion and height, and energy in the coil's field.
energy_account.why: Checks everything together: 953 mJ from the battery, found again to 4 · 10⁻⁷.
energy_account.step: The sources give the energy in a coil's field and the current in the circuit; the account only adds the items up.

one_picture.title: Through the hole: one picture
one_picture.setting: Looking exactly through the peephole, with no turn and no tilt.
one_picture.reads: A point (X, Y, Z) lands in the picture at (f·X/Z, f·Y/Z); every point on one line of sight lands in the same place.
one_picture.why: Checks that the skewed chair and the scattered rods give the chair's picture corner for corner: the pictures lie 10⁻¹⁶ apart, which is not at all.

straight_rods.title: Skewed, but straight
straight_rods.setting: The skewed chair: a point at ¼, ½ and ¾ along every rod.
straight_rods.reads: A projective map keeps straight lines: the skewed chair has straight rods that meet at the corners.
straight_rods.why: Checks the page's skew: the points lie 10⁻¹⁶ m off the rod, which is on it.

parallax.title: How far the eye may move
parallax.setting: The scattered rods; the eye moved sideways or up until the first corner opens by a minute of arc.
parallax.reads: Two points on one line of sight at d₁ and d₂ part by δ·sin φ·|1/d₁ − 1/d₂| when the eye moves by δ.
parallax.why: Checks the 0.16 mm the page gives: less than the peephole. The page finds it by halving, here is the formula; the two meet to 4 · 10⁻⁵.
parallax.step: The source gives how fast a point moves across the line of sight, V·sin φ/d. For two points the difference, for a small move δ in place of V·t.

second_eye.title: What the second eye sees
second_eye.setting: The scattered rods, the second eye 65 mm beside the first.
second_eye.reads: For small angles the corners part by b·sin φ·|1/d₁ − 1/d₂|.
second_eye.why: Checks the page's 6.6°, the reason for the single peephole. The formula is 1.7 % high, as 65 mm is no small step for rods half a metre away; the page works the angle out exactly.
second_eye.step: The source gives the disparity for small angles; the 65 mm are an adult's eye distance from the second (around 63 mm on average).

one_out.title: One in, one out
one_out.setting: Five balls 0.1 mm apart, no loss (e = 1), one lifted by 30° and let go; read after the first impact.
one_out.reads: At the bottom the first ball is as fast as a pendulum falling from 30°. With air between them, each ball meets its neighbour on its own; equal balls trade speeds, until the speed is in the last one.
one_out.why: Checks the pendulum and the impact at once: the last ball flies off at 0.63 m/s, as fast as the first came in. The 3 · 10⁻⁶ off: during the impact, gravity keeps pulling on the balls already leaving the bottom.
one_out.step: The first source gives the speed of a pendulum falling from θ₀ to the bottom. By the second, two equal balls trade speeds; with air between them that happens four times, one after the other.

momentum.title: Momentum is kept, losses and all
momentum.setting: The exhibit as it hangs: five balls touching, e = 0.95, one lifted by 30° and let go; read after the first impact.
momentum.reads: What one ball gives the other, it loses itself. The speeds after the impact add up to the speed the first came in at, even though the impact loses energy and not all of it goes into the last ball.
momentum.why: Checks that every force between two balls acts on both alike, the damping included. The 6 · 10⁻⁶ off is gravity, pulling during the impact on the balls moving off the bottom.
momentum.step: At the bottom, string and weight nearly cancel: during the short impact the row is nearly a closed system. With equal masses the sum of the momenta becomes the sum of the speeds; the first ball's speed is the second source's.

energy.title: Without losses, energy is kept
energy.setting: Five balls touching, no loss (e = 1), one lifted by 30° and let go; read after 2 s.
energy.reads: Every ball carries energy of motion and of height; a Hertz contact stores what it takes and gives it all back. Once none presses, the sum is the start's again: the height the first ball fell from.
energy.why: Checks the page's time loop, a millisecond a step and a microsecond while two balls touch: after 2 s the energy is the same to 10⁻⁵. What is off, the microsecond steps miss where a contact closes.
energy.step: The first source gives a pendulum's energy: ½v² + gL(1 − cos θ) stays the same. The second gives the Hertz contact an elastic energy that depends on the dent alone, so without damping it gives back all it takes. Summed over the balls, once none presses.

peak.title: The largest force, by Hertz
peak.setting: Five balls 0.1 mm apart, no loss (e = 1), one lifted by 30° and let go.
peak.reads: Two balls press on each other with a force growing as the dent to the power 3/2. The dent is deepest when all the pair's energy of motion is in it; there the force is largest.
peak.why: Checks Hertz's stiffness from Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio and the radius: 879 N at a dent of 18 µm. The page reads the force every microsecond, so just beside its top; hence the 4 · 10⁻⁵.
peak.step: The first source gives the force for any dent, the second the deepest dent when two balls meet; the one is put into the other. With air between them each pair meets on its own, and without loss each at the same speed.

duration.title: How long the impact lasts
duration.setting: Five balls 0.1 mm apart, no loss (e = 1), one lifted by 30° and let go.
duration.reads: With air between them the four pairs meet one after the other. Each contact lasts τ; in between, the ball just struck flies through the air left to the next.
duration.why: Checks the duration the page gives, from the first touch until the last contact opens: by hand 689 µs, 84 µs of it each contact; the page counts whole microseconds and makes it 688.
duration.step: The first source gives one contact's duration. The pair's centre moves at v/2, so at the end of its contact the ball struck is v·τ/2 further and flies the remaining air s − v·τ/2 at the speed v it took over by the second source. From touch to touch that is τ/2 + s/v, three times; then the last contact.

start.title: The first nudge grows
start.setting: Tap ρ = 28, brake σ = 10, as the page opens: the wheel from rest, full at the top, nudged by a hair; measured between 1.5 s and 2.5 s.
start.reads: From rest a small nudge grows at the larger eigenvalue of the equations at the standing wheel, (−1 − σ + √((1 − σ)² + 4ρσ))/2 per leak time 1/K.
start.why: Checks tap and brake in the time loop while the wheel has hardly moved: 2.37 per second, the nudge doubling every 0.29 s. The 3 · 10⁻⁵ off comes mostly from the second, dying share, not quite gone at 1.5 s.

steady.title: A little water: steady turning
steady.setting: Tap ρ = 5, brake σ = 10; the wheel from rest, read at the end of the 200 s the page shows.
steady.reads: Above ρ = 1 the wheel can turn steadily, at x = √(b(ρ − 1)) in units of the leaks; for the waterwheel b = 1.
steady.why: Checks the nonlinear terms and the wheel's b: 3.82 rpm. With Lorenz's b = 8/3 for the air it would be 6.24 rpm.
steady.step: The first source gives the steady turning of Lorenz's equations for any b; that b = 1 for the waterwheel is in the second. Back to the wheel: rate Ω = K·x, one turn is 2π.

threshold.title: The threshold of chaos
threshold.setting: Brake σ = 15 instead of 10; read off the tile “Chaos from a tap of”.
threshold.reads: Above ρ_H = σ(σ + b + 3)/(σ − b − 1) even steady turning is no longer stable.
threshold.why: Checks the threshold the page names, with the wheel's b: 21.9 at σ = 15. With Lorenz's b = 8/3 it would read 27.4.
threshold.step: The first two sources give the threshold for any b; put in is the waterwheel's b = 1 from the third.

volume.title: A volume of states shrinks
volume.setting: Tap ρ = 28, brake σ = 10: a tiny box of states, 2 · 10⁻⁵ wide, round the wheel's state after 20 s, run on for 2.5 s as the page runs it.
volume.reads: Lorenz's equations draw every volume of states together at the same pace, e^(−(σ + 1 + b)·K·t), wherever the wheel is.
volume.why: Checks the three dampings at once, brake, leaks and the wheel's b, in the middle of the chaos: after 2.5 s, 0.248 % of the volume is left. The 2 · 10⁻⁵ off is the Runge–Kutta method's error over these 50 steps.
volume.step: The sources give the shrinking for any b, in Lorenz's time τ; put in are the waterwheel's b = 1 from the third and τ = K·t.

wheel.title: The wheel's own equations
wheel.setting: Tap ρ = 28, brake σ = 10, as the page opens; read after 12 s, past the first two reversals.
wheel.reads: The water's spread turns with the wheel, water flows in at the top and leaks out everywhere; gravity turns the wheel, the axle brakes. Computed here in seconds, for a wheel of 0.5 m radius and a brake of 1 N·m·s.
wheel.why: Checks that Lorenz's equations with b = 1 are the wheel, turning into rpm included: 19.04 rpm after 12 s. Any other radius and brake with the same σ and ρ give the same number.
wheel.step: The source writes the brake as κ + Q_tot·R² and gravity on the tilted wheel as g·sin α; here they are ν and g. Inertia and inflow follow from σ = ν/(K·I) and ρ = π·g·r·q/(ν·K²).

textbook_lengths.title: The lengths by the textbook's formula
textbook_lengths.setting: Fifteen pendulums, a cycle of 60 s, the longest swinging 51 times in it; tuned for 0°, that is, by the formula for small swings.
textbook_lengths.reads: A pendulum that swings exactly N + n times in the cycle Γ has the period Γ/(N + n); T = 2π√(L/g) gives its length.
textbook_lengths.why: Checks how the row is tuned: the shortest pendulum swings 65 times in 60 s and is 21.1659 cm long. A miscounted number or another g would show here.

tuned_lengths.title: Tuned for 15°
tuned_lengths.setting: The page's row: fifteen pendulums, 60 s, the longest 51 times, tuned for 15°.
tuned_lengths.reads: A swing of 15° takes longer than a small one by the factor 2K/π. For it to take Γ/(N + n) all the same, the pendulum is shorter by the square of that factor.
tuned_lengths.why: Checks that the page tunes by the exact period, not by the textbook's formula: the longest pendulum is 34.0875 cm long. K is summed here as an integral, not by the arithmetic-geometric mean as in the engine.
tuned_lengths.step: The first source gives the length from the small swing's period, the second the period of any swing: 4K, in units of √(L/g); the third defines K as an integral. So the small swing's period to put in is Γ/(N + n)·π/(2K).

together.title: Together again after a cycle
together.setting: The page's row, let go at 15°; the clock at 60 s, one whole cycle.
together.reads: In the cycle every pendulum has made a whole number of swings and stands where it was let go.
together.why: Checks the page's clock over a whole minute: all fifteen stand at 15° again, none more than 10⁻¹²° off. The page computes each instant directly, without steps, so the sixtieth second is as exact as the first.

third.title: A third of the way through the cycle
third.setting: The page's row, let go at 15°; the clock at 20 s, a third of the cycle. Read at the second pendulum, which swings 52 times in the cycle.
third.reads: The second pendulum has made 17⅓ swings. The exact solution of the pendulum's equation, with Jacobi's function sn, says where it stands a third of a swing after its release.
third.why: Checks the shape of the swing between its turning points, not only how long it takes: −7.50807°, a little farther out than the half of 15° a cosine would give. sn is found here from its integral, not by the arithmetic-geometric mean as in the engine.
third.step: The first source gives the solution in a time measured in units of √(L/g), in which a swing takes 4K. After 17⅓ swings the argument is 17⅓·4K + K = 35·2K + K/3, so by the second source sn = −sin φ with F(φ) = K/3; the third gives F as an integral.

textbook_skew.title: Tuned by the textbook's formula
textbook_skew.setting: Fifteen pendulums, 60 s, the longest 51 times, tuned for 0° by the textbook's formula, but let go at 15°.
textbook_skew.reads: At 15° every swing takes longer by the factor 2K/π. The n-th pendulum manages only (N + n)·π/(2K) swings in the cycle; the shortest, with the most, falls behind the farthest.
textbook_skew.why: Checks the skew the page shows as its trick: the row comes back 21.5821° askew, the shortest pendulum that far behind the longest, in degrees of a swing.
textbook_skew.step: The first source gives the tuning, the second the period at 15°, the third K. In the cycle the n-th pendulum falls (N + n)(1 − π/(2K)) swings of 360° short; the shortest has c − 1 = 14 swings more than the longest.

at_rest.title: Standing still: the throw as a chord
at_rest.setting: The carousel at rest (0 rpm); the puck at 3 m/s, aimed 30° beside the other seat.
at_rest.reads: The puck goes straight, from the thrower's seat along a chord to the rim. The angle at the rim between the chord and the diameter is half the angle at the centre on the same arc: the puck arrives 2 · 30° = 60° beside the other seat.
at_rest.why: Checks which way the aim turns and where the page finds the rim: with no turning, only geometry is left. The page finds the rim by halving the flight time sixty times; the two meet to 10⁻⁹.
at_rest.step: With no force the puck goes straight (first source). Its path and the line to the other seat both start at the thrower's seat on the rim; by Euclid the angle at the centre, between the other seat and the path's end, is twice as large (second source).

straight_puck.title: The straight throw misses by 86°
straight_puck.setting: 6 rpm, radius 2 m; the puck at 3 m/s aimed straight at the other seat.
straight_puck.reads: Seen from outside the puck goes straight, with the throw u and, across it, the speed ΩR the thrower rides at. Its chord leans δ off the diameter and ends 2δ short of the other seat, which has meanwhile moved on by Ωt.
straight_puck.why: Checks both things that turn the throw aside: the thrower's own ride, δ = 22.7°, and the turning during the 1.13 s of flight. Together 86.3° clockwise, as the riders see it.
straight_puck.step: The first source gives the velocity seen from outside, v₀ = v + Ω × r: the throw and, across it, ΩR, so tan δ = ΩR/u. By Euclid the chord ends 2δ short of the other seat and is 2R·cos δ long, as the angle in a semicircle is right; at the speed √(u² + Ω²R²) the flight takes t. The rider turns it all back by −Ωt (fourth source).

coriolis_push.title: The Coriolis force as the puck leaves the hand
coriolis_push.setting: 6 rpm, radius 2 m; the puck at 3 m/s straight at the other seat, read at the moment of the throw, riding along.
coriolis_push.reads: A rider sees the puck pushed across the throw at 2Ωu: the Coriolis force per kilogram. At the throw the centrifugal force points outward along the line of the throw and adds nothing across it.
coriolis_push.why: Checks the turning back into the riders' view: 3.77 m/s² to the right, as an anticlockwise turn demands. Read off the page's path as a second derivative over three steps of 1 ms; the method is 7 · 10⁻⁷ off.
coriolis_push.step: The source gives the equation of motion in a uniformly turning frame; with no force, U = 0. At the moment of the throw v′ is the throw, square to Ω, and r′ is the seat, on the line of the throw: across it only 2Ωu is left.

ball_turn.title: The rolled ball turns at 2/7
ball_turn.setting: 6 rpm, radius 2 m; the rolling ball at 3 m/s straight at the other seat, seen from outside.
ball_turn.reads: Rolling, the ball must keep up with the plate under it. The friction that makes it do so turns its velocity steadily, at Ω/(1 + m r²/I), for a solid ball 2/7 of the platform's rate: seen from outside it runs on a circle.
ball_turn.why: Checks the rolling's factor: 10.29° a second, not the carousel's 36°. Read off the heading of the first and the last piece of the path drawn; on a circle every chord points exactly where the ball heads at the middle of its arc.

rayleigh.title: Blue scatters 4.4 times as strongly as red
rayleigh.setting: The tube as it is: 1 m long, cloudiness 1.5 per metre.
rayleigh.reads: Particles far smaller than the wavelength scatter inversely as the wavelength's fourth power: blue at 450 nm more strongly than red at 650 nm.
rayleigh.why: Checks the fourth power all the tube's colours come from: 4.353 times as strongly.

light_kept.title: No light is lost
light_kept.setting: The tube as it is: 1 m long, cloudiness 1.5 per metre; blue light, 450 nm.
light_kept.reads: What a stretch of the tube takes from the light, it scatters to the side there: β times the light still left. What goes to the side along the whole tube and what comes out at the end add up to all the lamp's light.
light_kept.why: Checks that the light at the side and the light at the end belong together: the side summed by Simpson's rule and the end added, 4 · 10⁻¹⁴ is missing, that is nothing.
light_kept.step: The source gives a thin slice's loss, μ·Φ·dz, and from it e^(−μd). Nothing is absorbed in the tube, so each slice's loss is what it scatters to the side. The page takes from that what the scattered light loses on its way to the wall, e^(−βa); here it is added back.

high_sun.title: A high sun, a flat air
high_sun.reads: With the sun high, the earth's curve does not matter: the light crosses the air slantwise, 1/sin h times as much as straight up.
high_sun.why: Checks the page's air mass, Kasten and Young's: 1.1540, not 1.1547. Their formula holds the curved air and the bending of the light, so it lies 6 · 10⁻⁴ lower; a mistake in the angle or its unit would stand out far.

sky_noon.title: The sky above the noon sun
sky_noon.setting: The sun straight overhead, 90°, no ozone layer; green light, 550 nm.
sky_noon.reads: The sky straight overhead is sunlight scattered once on its way down: scattered at every height and dimmed on the rest of the way. With the sun itself straight overhead, that is τ·e^(−τ).
sky_noon.why: Checks the page's sky at its limit: the formula turns 0/0 at m = 1, and the page computes it there specially. The 1.4 · 10⁻⁵ off: for the sun overhead the page takes Kasten and Young's air mass, which is not quite 1 there.
sky_noon.step: The source gives the light scattered once on its way down, for the sun at cosine μ_sw and the view at cosine μ. Looking straight up (μ = 1), with the sun at μ_sw = 1/m and at the bottom of the air (ζ = τ), that is (e^(−τ) − e^(−mτ))/(m − 1), per sunlight and per scattering into the view; its limit for μ → μ_sw gives τ·e^(−τ).

ozone_horizon.title: The ozone layer at the horizon
ozone_horizon.setting: The sun at the horizon, 0°, with the ozone layer.
ozone_horizon.reads: The ozone layer lies as a thin shell 22 km up. A ray from the horizon crosses it slantwise, but not endlessly as in a flat air: 12 times as much ozone as straight up.
ozone_horizon.why: Checks the path through the shell, by which the page dims the evening sun's orange: 12.064, by hand from the general integral, on the page from a formula rearranged; the two agree to 10⁻¹⁴.
ozone_horizon.step: The source gives the air mass for any density ρ(y) over the height y. With all the ozone in a thin shell at y = H, what is left of the integral is the fraction at H, over the same fraction straight up (z = 0). The zenith angle z is 90° less the sun's height.

lowest_tone.title: The lowest tone
lowest_tone.setting: The page's plate, 24 cm and 1 mm of steel; the shaker on the lowest tone it drives at the middle.
lowest_tone.reads: Leissa's table gives the free square plate λ = ωa²√(ρh/D) = 24.2702 for the lowest mode symmetric about both middle lines and both diagonals; in hertz f = λ/(2πa²)·√(D/(ρh)).
lowest_tone.why: Checks the Ritz method the page finds the modes by, and the turning into hertz: 102.43 Hz. Table and page meet to 4 · 10⁻⁸.

second_tone.title: The second tone, no overtone
second_tone.setting: The shaker on the second tone, 268.8 Hz.
second_tone.reads: By Leissa's table the second driven tone lies 63.6870/24.2702 times as high as the lowest, however large and thick the plate.
second_tone.why: Checks a higher mode, free of steel and size: 2.624 times as high, no whole multiple as on a string. The 1.4 · 10⁻⁵ off lies with the table: Iguchi's series is cut off after five terms, and the Ritz method never lies below the exact value, yet here lies below the table.

sharpness.title: How sharp a tone is
sharpness.setting: The shaker 0.2 Hz above the lowest tone, where the middle still swings 70.7 % as far as on the tone.
sharpness.reads: A tone is Δf = f/Q wide, measured where the energy falls to half; with the damping ζ, Q = 1/(2ζ).
sharpness.why: Checks the damping in the law the page makes the plate answer by: with ζ = 0.002, Q = 250, so the lowest tone is only 0.41 Hz wide.
sharpness.step: The source gives Q for a single oscillator. Near the lowest tone the plate swings almost only in this one shape; the other nine add 1.4 · 10⁻⁵.

fourth_tone.title: The fourth tone, weighed by its mass
fourth_tone.setting: The shaker on the fourth tone, 711.1 Hz; read off the tile for how far the middle swings.
fourth_tone.reads: On its tone each shape swings like a single oscillator, at the middle by φ(0)²·F/(μ·ω²·2ζ), with μ = ∫φ² the shape's mass. Against the lowest tone force and damping drop out.
fourth_tone.why: Checks that each shape enters with its own mass: 4.70 % of the lowest tone's. Without μ it would be 1.98 %, the first version's mistake. μ is integrated over the plate here, not summed as the squares of the coefficients as on the page.
fourth_tone.step: The source works a system of two masses: the answer is the sum of the shapes, and each answers on its tone with Q₁/K₁·1/(2ζ₁), Q₁ the force on the shape, K₁ its stiffness. For the plate the sum over the masses becomes an integral: K = μ·ω² and Q = φ(0)·F for a force at the middle. The shapes φ themselves are the page's.

same_height.title: As high on both sides
same_height.setting: A 1 m string, the peg 50 cm below the pivot, let go at 30°; for six seconds.
same_height.reads: The string pulls across the motion and does no work: round the peg the bob rises again to the height L(1 − cos θ₀) it was let go from.
same_height.why: Checks that the peg, catching the string, keeps the bob's speed and not its angular velocity: 13.3975 cm high. The page reads the bob every millisecond, and the turning point lies between two readings: hence the deviation of 2 · 10⁻⁷.

period.title: The period on two circles
period.setting: As above: a 1 m string, the peg 50 cm down, let go at 30°; timed from the first to the fourth time the peg catches the string.
period.reads: Out, the bob swings half a period on the whole string, back half a period round the peg, each at its own amplitude.
period.why: Checks both equations of motion and the switches between them, which the page finds within its step: 1.755778 s, to 10⁻⁹. K is summed here as an integral, not by the arithmetic-geometric mean as in the engine.
period.step: The first source gives ω = √(g/L), the second the pendulum's equation in the time ω·t and its period 4K, the third K. Half a period in seconds is thus 2√(ℓ/g)·K(sin(α/2)): once with ℓ = L and α = θ₀, once with ℓ = r and the amplitude φ₀ that reaches the same height round the peg.

loop.title: How deep the peg must be for the bob to loop
loop.setting: A 1 m string, let go from the horizontal, the peg 60 cm down: at the edge. The edge is found by halving between 55 and 65 cm.
loop.reads: At the top of the small circle the string must still pull. With the speed from the starting height that means h ≥ 5r/2; from the horizontal, h = 1 m, so r ≤ 40 cm, the peg at least 60 cm down.
loop.why: Checks the loop in the time loop itself, not the page's formula: from 59.99999 cm. With the peg a hair higher the string would be slack at the top only for an instant, shorter than a step; the page does not see that, hence the deviation of 2 · 10⁻⁷.
loop.step: The source gives the string's pull, mg(3cos θ − 2cos θ_m), for a pendulum turning at θ_m. Round the peg the radius is r, and the starting height stands in for cos θ_m: 1 − h/r. At the top, cos θ = −1, the pull is mg(2h/r − 5).

slack.title: Where the string goes slack
slack.setting: A 1 m string, the peg 55 cm down, let go from the horizontal: the case “Slack string”.
slack.reads: The string goes slack where its pull falls to zero: v²/r + g·cos φ = 0. With the speed from the starting height that is at the height (r + 2h)/3.
slack.why: Checks where the page lets the free flight begin: 81.6667 cm above the bottom, to 10⁻⁹, since the page finds the moment within its step.
slack.step: The source gives the pull mg(3cos θ − 2cos θ_m) for a pendulum turning at θ_m. Round the peg the starting height stands in for cos θ_m: 1 − h/r. Set to zero, that gives cos φ = 2(1 − h/r)/3, and the height r(1 − cos φ) = (r + 2h)/3.

winterthur.title: In Winterthur: 11.1° an hour
winterthur.setting: Winterthur, 47.5° north; the pendulum 12 m long, let go 50 cm out. Read at the first turning point after an hour.
winterthur.reads: The plane of the swing turns against the floor at Ω·sin φ, clockwise in the north: 360° · sin φ per turn of the Earth against the stars.
winterthur.why: Checks the swing drawn, not only the figure beside it: where the bob turns back after an hour, the plane lies turned 11.09° clockwise. The 2 · 10⁻⁸ off is the eighth digit of the Earth's turn the page takes, 7.2921150 · 10⁻⁵ per second.
winterthur.step: The first source gives the rate Ω·sin λ, the second its sense: clockwise in the north. For Ω stands one turn of the Earth against the stars, 86 164.0989 s (third source).

pole.title: At the North Pole: once round per turn of the Earth
pole.setting: At the North Pole, 90° north; otherwise as in Winterthur.
pole.reads: At the pole the pendulum keeps its plane against the stars, and the whole Earth turns away under it: once round in one turn of the Earth against the stars.
pole.why: Checks the Earth's turn the page takes: once round in 23.934 h, counted against the stars and not against the Sun.
pole.step: At the pole the Earth turns under the pendulum at its whole Ω (first source), once round against the stars in 86 164.0989 s (second source).

south.title: In Sydney: the other way
south.setting: Sydney, 33.9° south; otherwise as in Winterthur.
south.reads: South of the equator sin φ is negative: the plane turns anticlockwise.
south.why: Checks the latitude's sign in the page's figure "Per hour": −8.39°, that is 8.39° an hour anticlockwise.
south.step: The first source counts clockwise, and southern latitudes as negative. For the day stands, as above, one turn of the Earth against the stars (second source).

period.title: The beat of the swing
period.setting: Winterthur, the pendulum 12 m long; timed from the release to the turning point after an hour, over all the half swings between.
period.reads: A pendulum swinging little swings at T = 2π√(L/g), whatever its mass and swing.
period.why: Checks the length and gravity in the swing drawn: 6.9504 s. The Earth's turn changes it by only 2 · 10⁻⁹.

free_fall.title: The plastic plate falls freely
free_fall.setting: Field 0.15 T, magnets 20 mm high; your plate of plastic, no slots, 90 cm through the column.
free_fall.reads: What conducts no current is not braked: the plate falls freely from rest, s = ½·g·t².
free_fall.why: Checks that no brake is left without conductivity, and the column's drop: 0.43 s, as the fourth stopwatch above.

late_start.title: One time constant late
late_start.setting: The exhibit's slotted aluminium plate: 3 mm thick, teeth 8 mm high; field 0.15 T, magnets 20 mm high.
late_start.reads: With a brake proportional to the speed, the plate approaches its terminal speed v_E = m·g/c̄ exponentially, with the time constant τ = m/c̄. Soon it falls at v_E, τ behind a plate that had started at v_E.
late_start.why: Checks the fall, not the brake: with the page's mass and brake it is 1.710 s for 90 cm at 52.6 cm/s, and 54 ms more, 1.764 s in all. Without the time constant the time would be 3 % short.
late_start.step: The source gives the distance y = (mg/b)·t + (m²g/b²)·(e^(−bt/m) − 1), here with b = c̄. After 33 time constants the exponential is gone: y = v_E·(t − τ), so t = s/v_E + τ.

thickness.title: The thickness changes nothing
thickness.setting: Your plate of aluminium, no slots, 10 mm thick, not 3 mm; above, the exhibit's aluminium plate at 3 mm.
thickness.reads: A thicker plate carries more current and brakes harder, but it is heavier in the same measure: v_E and τ stay, and so does the whole fall.
thickness.why: Checks that the thickness enters the brake and the mass alike: both plates take 12.31 s, the same to 10⁻¹².
thickness.step: By the first source the current per area, J = σ(E + v×B), is the same in every layer of the plate; so the brake c̄ grows with the thickness d as the mass m = ϱ·d·A does. By the second, v_E = mg/c̄ and τ = m/c̄ depend only on their ratio.

metals.title: Copper against aluminium
metals.setting: Your plate of copper, no slots, 3 mm thick; then the same plate of aluminium, as the exhibit's.
metals.reads: For the same plate between the same magnets the terminal speeds go as resistivity times density: conducting well brakes, being heavy pulls.
metals.why: Checks the metals' values and how they enter: aluminium falls at 0.476 of copper's speed; the table itself rounds to 0.48. The 0.1 % off: the page computes with conductivities to three digits, the table gives resistivities to four.
metals.step: With J = σ(E + v×B) every current grows with σ while its pattern stays: the brake is σ·d·A·B₀²/2·η, with η from the shape alone. Set equal to the weight ϱ·d·A·g it gives v_E = ϱ·g/(σ·B₀²/2·η); for the same shape η drops out, and with σ = 1/ρ what is left is ρ·ϱ, the table's column.

strip.title: Fine teeth: the endless strip
strip.setting: Magnets 10 mm high, so a period of 20 mm; your plate of aluminium, 1 mm thick, slotted into teeth 2 mm high.
strip.reads: A tooth much wider than high carries current only across. No net current can flow across, so only what differs from the field's mean over the tooth drives: of an endless sheet's brake the share η = 1 − (sin(kh/2)/(kh/2))² is left.
strip.why: Checks why the slots take the brake away: by hand 3.25 % is left, the page computes 3.21 %. The 1.3 % off is the teeth's ends: the formula is for endlessly wide ones, the plate is 10 cm wide.
strip.step: The first source gives the current in a moving conductor, J = σ(E + v×B). In an endlessly wide tooth it flows only across, and as no net current can flow across, the field of the charges at the ends takes the mean B̄ away: J = σ·v·(B − B̄). By the second the heat equals the braking power; averaged over where the tooth stands against the poles, what is missing from B₀²/2 is B₀²/2·(sin(kh/2)/(kh/2))², the mean squared.

fall_time.title: The slow fall
fall_time.setting: The page's wheel: a solid disc, 0.5 kg, radius 6.5 cm, axle 5 mm, bands 60 cm long, without the bands' rubbing; the time until they are unwound.
fall_time.reads: The bands make the wheel turn as it falls. The axle being so thin, nearly all the energy of height goes into the spin, and the wheel falls as if in slow motion.
fall_time.why: Checks the rolling off the thin axle and the disc's moment of inertia: 3.2345 s for 60 cm, the same as the page's to 10⁻¹⁴.

pull.title: The bands carry nearly all the weight
pull.setting: As above, read after 1 s of falling.
pull.reads: Since the wheel falls so slowly, the bands pull with nearly all its weight; what is missing speeds the fall.
pull.why: Checks the bands' pull the page shows: 4.846 N.

back_up.title: Without rubbing, back to the top
back_up.setting: As above; read at the highest point after the first jerk.
back_up.reads: On the way down the energy of height becomes fall and spin, the jerk gives the speed back unchanged, and on the way up it all becomes energy of height again.
back_up.why: Checks that the fall, the jerk and the climb fit together: the wheel comes back to exactly 60 cm.
back_up.step: The first source gives the energy in the fall, MgL = ½Mv² + ½Iω². The jerk is a spring's swing whose energy, by the second, stays the same: the wheel leaves it as fast as it came. On the way up the first source's sum runs backwards.

jerk_time.title: The jerk: half a swing
jerk_time.setting: As above, the bands together at 10 kN/m; from the bands' end until the wheel climbs again.
jerk_time.reads: At the bottom it is no longer the rolling that slows the wheel but the bands, stretching: it swings half a swing on them as on a spring and turns back.
jerk_time.why: Checks the jerk, the time the bands pull hardest: 22.2 ms. The bands also catch the rest of the downward acceleration, so it lasts 1.4 · 10⁻³ longer than half a swing.
jerk_time.step: The source gives the period of a mass on a spring. The jerk is half of it, as long as the wheel comes in fast enough for its small downward acceleration not to count beside it.

peak.title: The largest pull in the jerk
peak.setting: As above, the bands together at 10 kN/m; the largest pull during the jerk.
peak.reads: Only the energy of the fall, ½Mv², goes into the bands, not the spin's: that runs on through the jerk. At the lowest point the bands pull with the weight and s·A besides.
peak.why: Checks the pull the page shows in the jerk: 31.14 N, more than six times the weight of 4.90 N.
peak.step: The first source gives the speed v at the bottom. In the jerk the wheel swings on the bands about the place where they carry its weight; by the second, at the lowest point the energy ½Mv² is all in the stretch A beyond that place: ½sA² = ½Mv².

milankovitch.title: The thinnest semicircle that stands
milankovitch.setting: A semicircle over 2 m, 40 stones, no load; the thickness lowered until no thrust line fits inside every stone.
milankovitch.reads: A semicircular arch of stones without mortar stands only if it is at least 0.1075 of its radius thick: so Milankovitch worked out, and Makris and Alexakis confirmed.
milankovitch.why: Checks that the page lays the thrust line inside the stones wherever it just still fits: with 40 stones the arch stands from 0.10743 of its radius. That is 6 · 10⁻⁴ less than Milankovitch's value, which holds for joints everywhere and is rounded to four places.

chain_push.title: The chain upside down pushes as it pulled
chain_push.setting: A catenary over 2 m, 1 m high, only 2 cm thick and of 40 stones, no load; the chain shown.
chain_push.reads: Turned upside down, the chain's pull becomes the arch's push. Across, the chain pulls the same everywhere, T₀ = w·a; up, each foot carries the weight of half the chain, w·a·sinh(c/a). So the push at the foot is 1/(2·sinh(c/a)) of the weight.
chain_push.why: Checks the page's figure "Push at the foot": 20.68 % of the weight. Forty straight stones 2 cm thick are no chain; their line is 1.3 · 10⁻⁴ off.
chain_push.step: The first source is Hooke's rule: as the chain hangs, the arch stands upside down. The second gives the chain: across T₀ = w·a, up w·s with s = a·sinh(x/a) from the vertex. So at the foot, x = c, stand w·a and w·a·sinh(c/a); a follows from the height, a·(cosh(c/a) − 1) = h.

weight.title: The stones' weight
weight.setting: The page's semicircle: 2 m span, 25 cm thick, 16 stones, 30 cm deep, 2400 kg/m³.
weight.reads: Every stone is cut along two radii π/16 apart: the triangle out to the outer edge less the triangle to the inner one, ½(R₊² − R₋²)·sin(π/16).
weight.why: Checks the stones the page takes its weights and centroids from: 561.86 kg, the page's figure "The arch's weight".
weight.step: The source gives a triangle's area from two sides and the angle between them. A stone is the triangle from the centre out to the outer edge, R₊ = R + t/2, less the one to the inner edge, R₋ = R − t/2; that times depth and density.

tone.title: The shortest rod's tone
tone.setting: The 50 cm rod, 2 mm steel; the table exactly in its beat.
tone.reads: A rod clamped at its foot swings at ω₀ = (β₁L)²/L²·√(EI/μ), β₁L = 0.596864π. Its weight presses it together and softens it: between no weight and Greenhill's buckling, ω² falls here along a straight line.
tone.why: Checks root, stiffness and weight in the tone the page writes under every rod: 5.58 Hz; the weight takes 2.5 % of ω². The page lowers ω² by Rayleigh 0.4 % more steeply than the line to Greenhill's exact buckling, hence 5 · 10⁻⁵.
tone.step: The first source gives the tone without weight, the second the length at which the rod buckles under its weight and its tone falls to nothing. In between, ω² is taken as a straight line in the load, an approximation; the tolerance carries it.

buckling.title: Too long for its weight
buckling.setting: A single rod of the same 2 mm steel, longer and longer, until the calculation refuses it because it buckles under its weight.
buckling.reads: A free-standing column buckles under its own weight once it is taller than (9B²/4·EI/(ρgA))^(1/3), B the first zero of the Bessel function J₋₁/₃.
buckling.why: Checks what the weight takes from the tone, where it takes all of it: 1.720 m by the source, 1.723 m by the page. The page works with the swinging shape, not the buckled one; that raises the buckling load by 0.4 % and the length by a third of that.

in_step.title: In step: the rod swings wide
in_step.setting: The table exactly in the 80 cm rod's beat, 2.09 Hz, 1 mm each way, damping 0.01; two minutes from rest.
in_step.reads: The table pushes the rod's swing with Γ·Ω²·Y, Γ = ∫φ/∫φ²; in step the tip swings steadily by Γ·Y/(2ζ).
in_step.why: Checks the time loop, the push and the damping: 78.3 mm from a 1 mm table. Γ = 1.566 is summed here from the source's shape, not taken from the engine.
in_step.step: The first source gives the driven oscillator, the second the shape of the swing, the third the participation factor for a shape of unit mass; for a shape of 1 at the tip it becomes ∫φ/∫φ².

neighbour.title: Beside it: the neighbour hardly stirs
neighbour.setting: As above; read off the 90 cm rod, whose own beat is 1.61 Hz.
neighbour.reads: The same formula out of step: Γ·r²·Y/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), r = Ω/ω.
neighbour.why: Checks that the table pushes with its acceleration, Ω²·Y, not with a fixed force: 3.86 mm; with the force ω²·Y it would be 2.30 mm. After two minutes 6 · 10⁻⁶ of the start is left.
neighbour.step: As above: the first source's driven oscillator, with the shape and the participation factor of the other two.

growth.title: From rest: how fast the swing grows
growth.setting: The table exactly in the 80 cm rod's beat, from rest; counted until the swing reaches 1 − 1/e of the steady one.
growth.reads: From rest the motion is the steady swing plus one dying away as e^(−ζωt); roughly it grows as 1 − e^(−ζωt), reaching 1 − 1/e after about 1/(2πζ) = 15.9 swings.
growth.why: Checks how the time loop joins damping and start: worked out exactly, 15.842 swings, 7.57 s at 2.09 Hz. The simple rule lies 0.5 % above, as the start itself has terms of size ζ.
growth.step: The source gives the solution as the steady swing plus a dying one at ω₁ = ω√(1 − ζ²) and the rate ζω; its two constants are chosen here so that place and speed start at zero.

kepler_period.title: Kepler’s third law in the funnel
kepler_period.setting: No rolling resistance, pushed at 36 cm at the circle’s speed, 0.4411 m/s (“Circle”); timing the first lap.
kepler_period.reads: On the circle the wall’s slope holds the ball towards the middle with (5/7)·g·k/r²: an inverse square like a star’s gravity. So Kepler’s T² = 4π²r³/(GM) holds, with (5/7)·g·k in place of GM.
kepler_period.why: Checks the motion towards the middle and the rolling ball’s share of 5/7: 5.127873 s for the lap. Sliding, without the 5/7, it would be quicker.
kepler_period.step: The first source gives Kepler’s law for a pull of GM/r² per kilogram. The second gives that a solid ball rolling on a slope feels only g·sin α/(1 + 2/5), 5/7 of sliding, with the solid ball’s moment of inertia 2/5·m·r² from the third. On the circle that share holds the ball: (v²/r)·cos α = (5/7)·g·sin α, and with tan α = k/r² that is v²/r = (5/7)·g·k/r².

equal_areas.title: Equal areas in equal times
equal_areas.setting: No rolling resistance, pushed at 36 cm along the rim at 0.30 m/s, slower than the circle; read after 20 s.
equal_areas.reads: The wall pushes in the plane through the axis, gravity pulls straight down: nothing turns the ball about the axis. So r²·φ̇ stays the same, twice the area the line to the middle sweeps in a second.
equal_areas.why: Checks the equation for going round, on a rosette that reaches far in and out again: after 20 s it is 0.108 m²/s, to 10⁻¹⁰, as at the push, 0.36 m times 0.30 m/s.
equal_areas.step: The source derives Kepler’s second law from the angular momentum being kept. Here it is the angular momentum about the axis, with the rolling ball’s spin (7/5)·r²·φ̇ per kilogram; the factor 7/5 is fixed, so r²·φ̇ stays.

energy.title: The energy is kept
energy.setting: As above: no rolling resistance, pushed at 36 cm at 0.30 m/s; after 20 s, 20,000 steps.
energy.reads: Without losses the sum of motion, spin and height stays the same; the solid ball’s spin carries 2/5 of what the motion carries.
energy.why: Checks the time loop over a rosette that turns a little further every lap: −0.209407 J/kg at the push and after 20 s, the same to 10⁻¹⁰.

brake.title: What the rolling resistance costs
brake.setting: Rolling resistance 0.002 as on the page, pushed at 36 cm on the circle; read over the first step.
brake.reads: The rolling resistance brakes with C·N against the motion; that costs C·N·v a second. N, the wall’s push, is the weight’s share across the wall and what holds the ball on its circle.
brake.why: Checks the brake and the wall’s push it comes from: 8.6625 mW per kilogram. Within the first millisecond the ball already slows a little and the brake with it, and below 1 mm/s the page fades the resistance out: together a deviation of 2 · 10⁻⁵.
brake.step: The first source gives the rolling resistance C·N. The second works the banked curve: N·sin θ = mv²/r and N·cos θ = mg. Added up across the wall they give N = mg·cos α + (mv²/r)·sin α; the grip of the rolling ball lies in the wall and adds nothing across it.

spacing.title: How far apart the stripes are
spacing.setting: The exhibit: a red laser, 650 nm, slits 0.25 mm apart and 0.05 mm wide, the wall 2 m behind; from the first dark stripe to the second.
spacing.reads: It is dark where the paths from the two slits differ by half a wavelength, one and a half, two and a half … At small angles the stripes lie λ·D/d apart.
spacing.why: Checks the slits' spacing in the pattern: 5.2 mm, measured on the pattern the page draws. The formula takes small angles, so the pattern lies 1.1 · 10⁻⁵ wider.
spacing.step: The source gives the dark stripes at d·sin θ = (m + ½)λ and, at small angles, the bright ones at y = mλD/d. The dark ones lie halfway between the bright ones, so just as far apart.

one_slit_dark.title: One slit alone: the first dark
one_slit_dark.setting: As above, one slit covered; the first dark beside the middle.
one_slit_dark.reads: One slit alone is dark where the paths from its two edges differ by a whole wavelength: every strip of the slit then has another that cancels it.
one_slit_dark.why: Checks the slit's width in the pattern: 26.002 mm beside the middle, as the page draws it.

quarter.title: One slit gives a quarter, not half
quarter.setting: As above, one slit covered; the brightness in the middle.
quarter.reads: In the middle the two waves arrive in step: their swings add to twice one, and the brightness is its square, four times one slit's.
quarter.why: Checks that the page adds the waves and squares after, rather than adding brightnesses: one slit 0.25 of the middle of two.
quarter.step: The first source gives that equal waves in step add their swings, the second that the brightness is the square: E² against (2E)².

first_bright.title: The first bright stripe is fainter
first_bright.setting: As above, both slits open; the brightness of the first bright stripe beside the middle.
first_bright.reads: Each slit alone grows darker to the side. The pair's first bright stripe lies at d·sin θ = λ, and there each slit gives only (sin β/β)² of its middle.
first_bright.why: Checks how the slits' width dims the stripes: 0.8751 of the middle for slits five times as far apart as they are wide.

missing.title: The fifth stripe is missing
missing.setting: As above, both slits open; the brightness where the fifth bright stripe would lie.
missing.reads: The slits lie five times as far apart as they are wide. Where the two reinforce each other for the fifth time, each alone is dark, and there is nothing to reinforce.
missing.why: Checks that the stripes and the dimming are computed at the same angle: 10⁻³³ there, that is dark.
missing.step: The first source gives the bright stripes at d·sin θ = mλ, the second a slit's dark at a·sin θ = λ. With d = 5a the fifth bright and the first dark coincide; the third calls this a missing order.

reserve.title: How much buoyancy is to spare
reserve.setting: The page's diver, 3 g of glass of 1.2 cm³ and 2 cm³ of air, at the surface, the hand not squeezing.
reserve.reads: It displaces water for its glass and its air; what that water weighs more than the glass keeps it up.
reserve.why: Checks the buoyancy the page shows as the reserve: 0.1936 g.

sinks_from_top.title: The squeeze that sinks it from the top
sinks_from_top.setting: The diver at the surface; the hand squeezes with 10.90 kPa. At 10.85 kPa it stays up.
sinks_from_top.reads: The hand's squeeze presses the bubble together (at one temperature p·V stays the same); it sinks once the bubble is smaller than m/ρ − V_g, the bubble it hovers with.
sinks_from_top.why: Checks Boyle and buoyancy in the page's time loop: 10.884 kPa, found as the squeeze from which a single step pulls it off the surface.
sinks_from_top.step: The first source gives p·V the same for the air, the second the balance of buoyancy and weight; together they give the squeeze at which the bubble at the surface just carries it.

rises_from_bottom.title: The squeeze below which it rises from the bottom
rises_from_bottom.setting: The diver lies on the bottom of the 30 cm bottle (squeeze hard first until it lies there); then 7.90 kPa. At 7.95 kPa it stays down.
rises_from_bottom.reads: Down there the water presses too, with ρ·g·H; it rises once the hand squeezes ρ·g·H less than the squeeze that sinks it at the top.
rises_from_bottom.why: Checks the water's pressure at depth: 7.947 kPa, 2.936 kPa less than at the top. Between the two squeezes the depth where it would hover lies in the bottle.
rises_from_bottom.step: As above, with the pressure at depth H from the third source.

leaves_hover.title: Why it does not hover
leaves_hover.setting: The hand squeezes with 10 kPa; the diver at rest a micrometre below the depth where it would hover, 9.03 cm; for five seconds.
leaves_hover.reads: A little deeper the bubble is a little smaller, and the missing buoyancy pulls it on: the distance grows as cosh(√k·t). What moves is the glass and the water it carries along, half its volume.
leaves_hover.why: Checks that hovering is unstable and how fast: the distance soon grows e-fold every 1.71 s. The 1 · 10⁻⁵ off comes from the water's drag and the curve of Boyle's law; both grow with the distance.
leaves_hover.step: The first source gives how the bubble shrinks with pressure, the second the pressure at depth; for a small step δz the change is linear. The third gives the water a sphere carries along, half its volume, which the page takes over for the tube.

axis_path.title: The axis falls, the rails rise
axis_path.setting: The standard exhibit: radius 6 cm, cone angle 20°, spread 20°, slope 4°, rails 30 cm long and 6 cm apart at the bottom.
axis_path.reads: The line from the axis to the contact is tilted by the angle δ, with sin δ = tan β·cos γ·tan α. So the axis runs on a straight line that falls by δ − γ.
axis_path.why: Checks the exact contact, which the engine finds another way, by the rail's distance from the cone: over 30 cm the axis falls by 1.88426 cm; the two ways meet to 10⁻¹².
axis_path.step: The source measures its angles in the rails' plane and calls δ its α. That plane rises at γ; a rail that spreads by tan β per metre seen from above spreads by tan β·cos γ in the plane. With tan φ = tan β·cos γ and the cone angle α as ψ, sin δ follows, and seen from above the axis falls over the length l by l·tan(δ − γ).

threshold.title: The boundary between up and down
threshold.setting: The standard exhibit's cone and spread; the slope at which the axis keeps the same height all along is found by halving between 0° and 15°.
threshold.reads: The cone rolls up as long as δ is greater than the slope γ; at the boundary the two are equal. That gives the textbook's condition tan γ* = tan α·tan β, here exactly.
threshold.why: Checks the boundary the page names: 7.54628°. It is found on the engine's exact contact, not with the page's formula; the two meet to 10⁻¹².
threshold.step: The first source gives the condition sin(δ − γ) > 0, at the boundary therefore δ = γ; the second sin δ = tan φ·tan ψ, converted as above to tan β·cos γ·tan α. With δ = γ, sin γ = tan β·cos γ·tan α, so tan γ = tan α·tan β.

speed.title: The speed from the energy
speed.setting: The standard exhibit, let go at the low end; read after one second.
speed.reads: What the axis loses in height becomes motion and spin: ½(1 + I/(M a²))·v² = g·Δz, with a the radius the cone rolls on, and I = (3/10)·M·R² for two solid cones.
speed.why: Checks the time loop and the rolling on the shrinking radius a: 28.5357 cm/s after one second, to 10⁻⁹. The higher up, the more of the energy is in the spin.
speed.step: The first source gives the energy and, with its equations (7) and (8), where the axis is and on what radius a the cone rolls, the angles converted as above to the view from above. The second gives a cone's moment of inertia; two equal cones, base to base, have the same I/(M·R²).

beat_rate.title: As many beats as the difference
beat_rate.setting: The rider, 1 g on each prong, 30 % up from the root; both forks struck together, for ten seconds.
beat_rate.reads: Two tones together are the mean tone times a slow envelope, which falls silent |f₂ − f₁| times a second.
beat_rate.why: Checks the sound the page draws and plays: 0.8173 silences a second, one every 1.22 s, as many as the difference of the two pitches. Read at the crests of the mean tone, where the sum equals the envelope.

tip_rider.title: The rider at the tip
tip_rider.setting: 1 g on each prong, right at the tip.
tip_rider.reads: A prong swings like a clamped beam in its first mode. At its tip it acts as if a quarter of its mass sat there, and the rider adds in full. The same stiffness carries more mass: f = f₀·√(M*/(M* + m)).
tip_rider.why: Checks the mass a prong counts with at its tip: 5 g of its 20 g; the fork drops from 440 Hz to 401.66 Hz. Here the quarter is summed over the mode's shape; the page puts in ¼.
tip_rider.step: The first source gives the shape of a clamped beam's first mode, the second how a mass as felt is found from the energy of motion: M* = M·∫φ², with φ = 1 at the tip. A rider at s counts with m·φ(s)². At the same stiffness the frequency goes with 1/√mass.

rider_on_prong.title: The rider further down
rider_on_prong.setting: 1 g on each prong, 30 % of the way from the root to the tip, as the page starts.
rider_on_prong.reads: Further down the prong moves less: the rider counts only with φ(s)², the square of the mode's shape where it sits.
rider_on_prong.why: Checks the mode's shape inside the prong: the second fork sounds at 439.18 Hz instead of 440 Hz.
rider_on_prong.step: As for the rider at the tip, with φ(0.3) from the first source's mode shape, scaled so that φ is 1 at the tip.

centre.title: The middle sinks
centre.setting: Vessel Ø 30 cm, 30 cm high, filled 10 cm deep; turntable at 90 turns a minute.
centre.reads: Water turning as one body has a paraboloid for its surface. As the water does not become more, the middle sinks ω²R²/(4g) below the depth at rest.
centre.why: Checks the shape and the volume together: 4.91 cm of the 10 cm of water are left at the middle.

dry_rate.title: When the middle runs dry
dry_rate.setting: The same vessel; turntable at 126 turns a minute, just short of the limit.
dry_rate.reads: The middle reaches the bottom once it has sunk by the whole depth at rest: at ω₁ = (2/R)·√(h·g).
dry_rate.why: Checks the limit at which the page turns from a bowl to a ring: ω₁ = 13.20 a second, 126.1 turns a minute.

dry_rim.title: Dry in the middle: the rim
dry_rim.setting: The same vessel; turntable at 160 turns a minute, past the limit of 126.
dry_rim.reads: With the middle dry, the water stands in a ring round a dry patch of radius δ. The surface is the same paraboloid, set lower; at the wall it stands α·(R² − δ²) high.
dry_rim.why: Checks the page's second case, where the dry patch, not the depth at the middle, keeps the volume: 25.38 cm at the rim. The page computes R·ω·√(h/g), the way here goes through δ; the two meet but for rounding.
dry_rim.step: The source gives the dry patch's radius δ and the surface z = α·(r² − δ²); at the wall r = R.

mirror.title: The bowl as a mirror
mirror.setting: The same vessel; turntable at 7 turns a minute, one turn in 8.6 s.
mirror.reads: A dish that is D deep out to a distance r gathers light coming straight down at f = r²/(4D). The water has D = α·r², so f = 1/(4α) = g/(2ω²), whatever the vessel's size.
mirror.why: Checks the focal length the page shows: 9.13 m above the bowl's lowest point.

spin_up.title: The water lags behind
spin_up.setting: The same vessel; turntable switched from rest to 90 turns a minute, the water at rest. Read after one spin-up time, at the page's step of 10 ms.
spin_up.reads: The bottom drags the water along through a thin boundary layer. After the spin-up time τ = h/√(ν·ω_v) it still lacks the share 1/e of the vessel's speed.
spin_up.why: Checks the page's time loop and spin-up time: after 32.58 s the water turns at 63.2 % of the vessel's speed, 56.9 of 90 turns a minute.
spin_up.step: The source does a closed cylinder 2L high, with one Ekman layer at the bottom and one at the top. By symmetry its middle plane carries no shear, as a flat free surface does: water h deep is the lower half, L = h. The source does small changes; the page lets large ones lag the same way, with Ω the larger of the two speeds.

lift.title: The load the ring carries
lift.setting: The page's ring (10 cm across, a 3 cm hole, 1.5 cm high, ferrite) and the top's magnet of 0.64 A·m²; the load 4.6 cm above the ring.
lift.reads: The top stands against the field and is pushed towards where it is weaker: upwards, with μ times the field's slope. The ring's field is summed here loop by loop.
lift.why: Checks the ring's field on its axis, which everything else comes from: a load of 23.589 g at 4.6 cm. The page computes the field in closed form, here it is summed; the two agree to 10⁻¹².
lift.step: The second source turns the magnetisation M into a current of M per metre of height round the ring's outer wall and the opposite one round its hole. Each thin layer of it is a loop; the first source gives its field on the axis, summed here over the ring's height and differentiated in z. The third gives the energy mgz + μB, and so the force −μB′.

window_foot.title: The window's foot
window_foot.setting: The page's ring; the lowest height a top can float at.
window_foot.reads: Up and down the top holds only where the field falls ever more slowly upwards, B″ > 0. The limit is the field's inflection point, B″ = 0.
window_foot.why: Checks the window's lower end: 4.3587 cm, as the page finds it by its grid and bisection.
window_foot.step: The first source gives the conditions and says the window begins at the inflection point. B″ comes here from the field summed loop by loop (second and third sources), its zero by bisection.

window_head.title: The window's head
window_head.setting: The page's ring; the highest height a top can float at.
window_head.reads: Sideways the top holds only while B′² > 2·B·B″; above, it slides off to the side.
window_head.why: Checks the window's upper end: 4.8052 cm. The window is thus only 4.5 mm high.
window_head.step: The first source gives the condition for holding sideways. B, B′ and B″ come here from the field summed loop by loop, the limit by bisection.

bob.title: Bobbing up and down
bob.setting: The page's top, 23.5 g, no warming; where it floats.
bob.reads: Where the weight meets the load, the energy mgz + μB is lowest. Its curvature μB″ acts as a spring, and the top bobs at that spring's frequency.
bob.why: Checks the bobbing frequency the page gives: 1.466 Hz, at the height found here in the summed field.
bob.step: The first source gives the energy mgz + μB. Its second derivative in height is μB″, the spring constant; the second gives ω = √(k/m).

drift.title: Drifting round the axis
drift.setting: The page's top, 23.5 g, no warming; where it floats.
drift.reads: Beside the axis the field is stronger, by r²(B′² − 2BB″)/(8B). The top is pushed back towards the axis and slowly circles it.
drift.why: Checks how the page gets the field beside the axis from the field on it: 0.636 Hz.
drift.step: The first source gives the field's square beside the axis from the derivatives on it. Its square root for small r is B + r²(B′² − 2BB″)/(8B); differentiated twice in r and times μ that is the spring constant sideways, and the third source gives the frequency.

period.title: There and back once
period.setting: The page's circuit: 200 H, 125 µF, 90 Ω, 10 V; the switch thrown.
period.reads: A circuit with resistance swings at ω′ = √(1/LC − (R/2L)²), a little slower than without.
period.why: Checks the time the needle takes there and back: 0.9941 s, measured between its first and third pass through zero.

energy_kept.title: What one swing keeps of the energy
energy_kept.setting: As above; compared are the moment of the throw and one period later.
energy_kept.reads: After one period the charge is back, only e^(−RT/2L) times as large, and the current is zero: the energy q²/2C has fallen to e^(−RT/L).
energy_kept.why: Checks that decay and swing fit together: 63.9 % stays in capacitor and coil. Were the page's period off, the current would not be at zero a period later, and the share would differ.
energy_kept.step: The first source gives the charge, the second the energy in capacitor and coil. After a full period the cosine repeats, only e^(−RT/2L) smaller.

energy_account.title: No energy goes missing
energy_account.setting: As above; ten seconds after the throw.
energy_account.reads: What is missing from capacitor and coil has become heat in the wire, at the power R·i².
energy_account.why: Checks the page's bar, which shows the heat as what is left: 6.25 mJ from the battery, after 10 s still 1.1 % of it in capacitor and coil; the rest is the heat, summed here over the current, to 3 · 10⁻¹⁴.
energy_account.step: The first source says how fast the wire eats the energy, the second what it consists of; summed over time that gives the account.

edge.title: At the edge: it swings no more
edge.setting: Resistance 2√(L/C) = 2529.8 Ω instead of 90 Ω, otherwise as above.
edge.reads: At R = 2√(L/C) the two roots coincide; from rest the current is q₀ω₀²·t·e^(−ω₀t), strongest after 1/ω₀ at q₀ω₀/e.
edge.why: Checks the branch of the calculation the page takes at the edge: 2.908 mA after 0.158 s. On the slider it is 2530 Ω, just above; there the peak lies 5 · 10⁻⁵ lower.
edge.step: The first source gives the edge, where √(1/LC) = R/2L, the second the solutions e^(st) with s = −ω₀(ζ ± i√(1 − ζ²)). At the edge ζ = 1, and both s are −ω₀; the second solution is then t·e^(−ω₀t). Started from rest, the formula follows.

line.title: The line: the inclined plane
line.setting: A solid ball, 50 cm down and 120 cm along to the finish.
line.reads: On the straight track the ball rolls with a fixed acceleration g′·H/L, from rest: L = ½·a·T².
line.why: Checks the sum over ds/v by which the page computes every track, in its simplest case: 0.982374 s. After the page's substitution the summand is constant here, so the sum is right but for rounding.
line.step: The first source gives a rolling ball’s acceleration on an incline, g·sin θ/(1 + 2/5), with sin θ = H/L; the second the distance from rest, L = ½·a·T², with L² = D² + H²; the third the solid ball’s moment of inertia, 2/5·m·r².

cycloid.title: The cycloid: the fastest track
cycloid.setting: As above: a solid ball, 50 cm down, 120 cm along.
cycloid.reads: On the cycloid x = r(φ − sin φ), y = r(1 − cos φ) the rolling circle’s angle runs evenly with time: φ = t·√(g′/r). At the finish it is φ_B.
cycloid.why: Checks the fastest track and how the page lays its cycloid through the finish: 0.747261 s. Near the cusp at the start 1 − cos φ loses digits, hence 3 · 10⁻¹¹.
cycloid.step: The first source works a body sliding without friction under g. The rolling ball feels only g′ = g/(1 + 2/5) along any track, which the second gives; so ω = √(g′/r). φ_B is the angle at which the cycloid’s run and drop stand as 120 to 50.

tautochrone.title: The cycloid valley: as long from anywhere
tautochrone.setting: The page’s valley, radius 30 cm, a solid ball; read at the highest, let go 59 cm above the bottom.
tautochrone.reads: In a cycloid valley a ball needs π·√(r/g′) to the bottom, wherever it is let go.
tautochrone.why: Checks the time table by which the page runs the balls in the valley: 0.650151 s from 59 cm too. The page’s sum over 1440 steps is 7 · 10⁻⁸ off, an error that falls with the square of the step.
tautochrone.step: The first source gives the time for a body sliding without friction under g; the rolling ball feels g′ = g/(1 + 2/5), which the second gives.

bowl.title: The circular bowl beside it: wider is slower
bowl.setting: The circular bowl beside the valley, radius 1.2 m, four times the cycloid’s radius; the solid ball from 59 cm up.
bowl.reads: In the bowl the ball swings like a pendulum of length R under g′; it needs a quarter of its period to the bottom, √(R/g′)·K(sin(φ₀/2)).
bowl.why: Checks the bowl by which the page shows that only the cycloid brings them all in together: 0.696484 s from 59 cm, later than in the valley. K is summed here as an integral; the page’s sum is 5 · 10⁻⁸ off.
bowl.step: The first source gives the pendulum’s period, 4K in units of √(R/g′), the second K, the third g′ = g/(1 + 2/5) for the rolling ball. The bowl has the radius 4r, the cycloid’s curvature at its bottom, and the ball starts at the same height h as in the valley: cos φ₀ = 1 − h/R.
