overview.why: Behind every exhibit stands a differential equation. This course is its ground: what such an equation is, where it comes from, and what it says about a real system.
overview.how: Every lesson follows the same pattern: a question from practice, the model that answers it, experiments you run with sliders, what they showed, and exercises — estimate first, then calculate. Every number is computed by the app's own engine and checked against reference values.
overview.lessons_hint: Your progress is kept on this device only.
overview.surprises_hint: Every estimate that was more than half off — the list worth reading back.
overview.no_surprises: None yet. Estimate before you calculate, and the ones that surprise you will collect here.

recipe.title: The recipe: eight steps
recipe.hint: Every model in this course is written by these steps.

question.title: Clarify the question
question.body: What must the model answer, and to what accuracy? A model without a question has no way of being right.

boundary.title: System boundary and assumptions
boundary.body: Decide what is inside, what is outside, and what is neglected — and write it down.

coordinate.title: Choose a coordinate and reduce
coordinate.body: One coordinate per degree of freedom, everything else reduced onto it through the transmissions.

balance.title: Write the balance
balance.body: Change = inflow − outflow: of mass, energy, momentum or gas. This is where the differential equation comes from.

normalise.title: Normalise
normalise.body: Bring it into a standard form — τ, ω₀, D — so it can be compared with every other system of its kind.

solve.title: Solve
solve.body: In closed form where there is one, numerically where there is not.

check.title: Check
check.body: Units, limits, a hand estimate, a measurement. A result nobody has checked is a guess with decimals.

interpret.title: Interpret
interpret.body: Translate the answer back into the question's terms: a time, a force, a design decision.

tank.title: A balance becomes a first-order lag
tank.hint: A tank with a constant inflow and an outflow that grows with the level. Change the inflow, the area or the outlet and watch the level settle.
tank.insight: The balance A·dh/dt = inflow − k·h is a first-order lag with τ = A/k: a bigger tank or a narrower outlet makes it slower, and it settles where outflow equals inflow.

exercise.estimate_why: Estimate first: the answer field opens once you have committed to a number.
exercise.wrong: Not yet — try again, or take a hint.
exercise.surprise: Your estimate was {{pct}} % off: noted under Surprises.

animation.slow: Slow motion: one period every two seconds, whatever the frequency.

first_order.question: A temperature sensor is dipped from 20 °C into an 80 °C bath. When can you trust its reading — and what does it show after eight seconds?
first_order.model: One store (the sensor's heat capacity) and one resistance (the transfer from the bath into it): whatever flows in raises the store, and the flow is proportional to the difference that is left. Written as a balance, that is a first-order lag:
first_order.model_tau: τ is the time constant. After one τ the response has covered 63 % of the way, after three 95 %, after five 99.3 % — whatever the system is made of.

assumptions.one_store: One store: the sensor is at one temperature throughout, with no gradient inside it.
assumptions.linear: Linear: the flow is proportional to the difference, so τ does not depend on how far it has to go.
assumptions.constant: Constant parameters: τ is the same at 20 °C as at 80 °C.

insights.settled: After 5 τ the response has covered 99.3 % of the step: settled, for every first-order system.
insights.read: τ is read off a measurement where the response has covered 63 % — or where the starting tangent reaches the final value.
insights.log: On a logarithmic axis the remaining distance is a straight line: the slope is −1/τ, and a measurement that is not straight there is not first order.

step.title: The step response
step.hint: Move τ and the two levels. The marks are at 1, 2, 3 and 5 τ; the dashed line is the starting tangent, which reaches the final value at exactly τ.

first_order.fraction_at: Share of the step at t

measure.title: Read τ off a measurement
measure.hint: A noisy measurement with a time constant you do not know. Click the curve where it crosses the 63 % line (or set the marker below), then compare.
measure.marker_hint: Where the measurement crosses the 63 % line, the time is τ.
measure.result: You read {{yours}} s; the true τ is {{truth}} s ({{off}} % off).

second_order.question: A torque measuring shaft is struck once and rings. How fast does it ring, how quickly does it calm down — and how far off does a measurement read when the signal comes close to its natural frequency?
second_order.model: An inertia on a spring with a damper: Newton's law for rotation. Two numbers say everything about it — the natural frequency ω₀ and the damping ratio D.
second_order.model_magnification: Driven at a frequency f, the response is the static one times the magnification V(η); and two successive maxima of a free decay give D without knowing the inertia or the stiffness:

assumptions.lumped: One lumped inertia: the shaft's own distributed mass is left out, which is the first mode of it and the one a measuring chain cares about.
assumptions.viscous: Viscous damping, proportional to the speed; no friction that stays the same size.
assumptions.linear: A linear spring over the whole travel.

insights.peak: D = 0.05 means a magnification of 10 at f₀: the shaft rings up to ten times its static deflection.
insights.chain: A measuring chain reads within about 4 % up to a fifth of its natural frequency: f₀ ≥ 5 × the highest frequency of interest.
insights.mass: More inertia at the same damper lowers D as well as f₀, because D = d/(2√(c·J)).

system.title: The step response
system.hint: Set the shaft by its parts or by its two numbers. The dashed lines are the envelope e^(−Dω₀t); the colour of the chip says which of the three solutions it is.

second_order.torque_note: Driven by a torque step of {{torque}} N·m.

magnification.title: Magnification and the error of a measuring chain
magnification.hint: V(η) for your damping (bold) and five references. Move the excitation and read how much more the shaft moves than its static deflection — which is how far a measuring chain built on it misreads.

decay.title: Damping from a decay test
decay.hint: A struck shaft, measured with noise; its damping is unknown. Click two successive maxima to compute Λ and D, then compare.
decay.not_successive: Pick two maxima next to each other.
decay.result: Your two maxima give D = {{yours}}; the true D is {{truth}}. Read over all {{n}} periods at once, D = {{overall}} — one logarithm over many periods is the steadier answer.

eigenvalues.question: What do the two numbers a second-order system is solved for actually say — and what is a system with two coupled states doing when it moves?
eigenvalues.model: A linear system ẋ = A·x moves as a sum of its eigensolutions: each eigenvalue λ is how fast one part decays or grows and how fast it turns, each eigenvector the direction it moves in.
eigenvalues.model_pair: For a mass on a spring with a damper the matrix has a pair of eigenvalues, and they are exactly the roots of lesson 2's characteristic equation:

assumptions.linear: Linear and time-invariant: A is constant. A nonlinear system has eigenvalues only around an operating point.
assumptions.minimal: Poles and eigenvalues coincide when the system is written without cancelling factors; a pole that a zero cancels is still an eigenvalue of A.

insights.parts: λ = σ ± jω: the real part σ sets the envelope e^(σt), the imaginary part the ringing frequency.
insights.same: det(A − λI) = 0 is the characteristic equation of lesson 2: poles, eigenvalues and its roots are the same numbers.
insights.vectors: A trajectory that starts on a real eigenvector stays on that straight line; every other is a mix of the two directions.

scalar.title: One eigenvalue: ẋ = a·x
scalar.hint: Move a through zero: negative decays, positive grows, and the time constant or the doubling time is 1/|a| apart from a factor.

poles.title: Poles and the step response
poles.hint: Set f₀ and D, or drag the upper pole in the plane. The dashed half circle is |λ| = ω₀; a pair on it differs only in damping.

matrix.title: A 2×2 system and its phase portrait
matrix.hint: Edit the matrix or start from a preset. The dashed lines are the real eigenvectors; twelve trajectories start on the dotted unit circle.

laplace.question: A measurement chain is a shaft behind a filter behind an amplifier. What does the chain do to a 3 Hz signal — how much smaller, and how much later does it arrive?
laplace.model: The Laplace transform turns differentiating into multiplying by s, so a differential equation becomes an algebraic one. Each block is a transfer function G(s); blocks in series multiply, and on a Bode plot in decibels they add.
laplace.model_delay: At a frequency f, a phase lag is a delay:

assumptions.lti: Linear and time-invariant blocks; a saturating amplifier is not a transfer function.
assumptions.steady: Bode describes the steady state under a sine; the start-up is the step response's business.
assumptions.dead_time: A dead time adds phase but no pole: e^(−sT) has none, and none is drawn.

insights.product: Blocks in series multiply; on a Bode plot in dB their curves add — the dashed curves sum to the solid one.
insights.final: The final value of a stable step response is G(0): read off the transfer function without solving anything.
insights.lag: A PT1 delays low frequencies by about τ: behind a 5 Hz filter a 3 Hz signal arrives 28.7 ms late, behind a 50 Hz filter a 5 Hz signal 3.2 ms.
insights.filter: Filter torque and angle identically — or offline, forward and backward — or the filter draws a hysteresis the test object does not have.

steps.title: Laplace, step by step
steps.hint: The first-order step solved the Laplace way: every line carries your numbers.

chain.title: A Bode construction kit
chain.hint: Up to four blocks in a chain. The total is solid, each block dashed under it; the cursor reads gain, phase and the delay the phase means.

filter.title: The hysteresis a filter invents
filter.hint: A test object with no hysteresis (torque proportional to angle), swept sinusoidally. Filter only the torque and a loop appears; filter both, or offline, and it is gone. Add friction to see a real one survive.

numerics.question: Most equations in practice have no closed-form solution, so a computer steps through them. How large may the step be — and what does a method do to the system it is stepping?
numerics.model: Euler takes the slope at the start of each step and holds it for the whole step. RK4 evaluates the slope four times inside the step and takes a weighted mean:
numerics.model_stability: On ẏ = λy a method multiplies the solution by a fixed factor each step, and it is stable only while that factor's size is at most one. For Euler:

assumptions.fixed: A fixed step: the methods here do not adapt it. An adaptive method (like the one the pump-down runs on) chooses its own.
assumptions.rounding: Rounding is ignored: in double precision it is far below every error shown here.

insights.order: Euler's error falls with h, RK4's with h⁴: halving the step halves one and divides the other by sixteen.
insights.energy: Euler pumps energy into an oscillator: at h·ω₀ = 2D it cancels the damping exactly — on the measuring shaft that is h = 1 ms, which keeps it ringing at its full 1° for ever — and above it the shaft rings up.
insights.rule: Rule of thumb for RK4: h at most a twentieth of the shortest period. Explicit Euler on a lightly damped oscillator needs h·ω₀ < 2D, which at D = 0.05 is a sixty-third of a period.
insights.stiff: Stiff means fast and slow dynamics together: a 1 ms lag beside a 10 s one forces RK4 into more than 10,000 steps over 30 s for a part that is gone after 5 ms. Implicit Euler is stable at any step.

sensor.title: Euler, Heun and RK4 against the exact solution
sensor.hint: The sensor of lesson 1 (τ = 4 s, 20 → 80 °C). Make the step larger — past τ Euler overshoots, past 2τ it runs away.

regime.one_step: Euler lands in one step (h = τ)

errors.title: Error table
errors.hint: Every step's value and its error.

rk4_table.title: RK4 step by step
rk4_table.hint: Where each of the four slopes is evaluated, and what it is.

oscillator.title: Energy drift on an oscillator
oscillator.hint: The measuring shaft of lesson 2 (f₀ = 15.9 Hz, D = 0.05) released from 1°, one second, four methods. Above, the amplitude on a logarithmic axis; below, the angle.
oscillator.neutral: Step at which Euler cancels the damping

stiff.title: Stiffness
stiff.hint: Two independent lags, 1 ms and 10 s, over 30 s. Shown is the slow one. Make the step larger than 2.8 ms and RK4 diverges; implicit Euler stays stable at any step.

two_mass.question: A torque measuring shaft sits between the motor and a heavy adapter on the test object. Why does it read 15 % too little at 3 Hz?
two_mass.model: Two inertias on two springs: the motor J₁, the measuring shaft c₁, the column or adapter J₂, the test object as a torsion bar c₂ to ground. In matrix form:
two_mass.model_reading: The shaft reads the torque across itself; the test object carries the torque across the bar. Between the two sits J₂, and what it takes to accelerate it is in the reading and not in the test object:

assumptions.lumped: Lumped inertias: the shaft's own inertia is left out (split between its ends it would shift both modes by a few percent).
assumptions.torque: An ideal torque drive: the motor's current loop is not modelled.

insights.count: n inertias on springs tied to ground give n natural frequencies; a free chain adds a rigid-body motion at 0 Hz.
insights.soft: The low mode is everything swinging on the softest spring: all inertia on the two springs in series gives 6.3 Hz by hand, against 6.94 Hz exact.
insights.error: The shaft reads about 1 − (f/f_a)² times what the test object carries, with f_a = √(c₂/J₂)/2π: 2 % too little at 1 Hz, 15 % at 3 Hz, 43 % at 5 Hz with the default adapter.

rig.title: The rig under a sinusoidal drive
rig.hint: Move the excitation or jump to a preset. The discs turn in slow motion with the phases the engine computed; the bars show how much each spring is twisted.

two_mass.parameters_hint: Inertias, stiffnesses and dampings, each on a slider.
two_mass.animation_label: The two inertias at {{f}} Hz, in slow motion
two_mass.object_carries: What the test object carries, M_T

compensation.title: Compensating the adapter's inertia
compensation.hint: M_T = M_W − J₂·φ̈₂, with the acceleration from the measured angle differentiated twice. Raise the noise: the correction amplifies it by the square of the sample rate, and a filter trades that against lag.

trap.inertia: An inertia between the torque sensor and the test object is in the reading: the error grows with (f/f_a)².
trap.filter: Filter torque and angle identically, or the filter invents a hysteresis.

pt1_reading.title: A sensor's reading
pt1_reading.prompt: A sensor with τ = {{tau}} s is stepped from {{start}} °C to {{final}} °C. What does it read after {{t}} s?
pt1_reading.hint1: After t/τ time constants, the share e^(−t/τ) of the step is still missing.
pt1_reading.solution: {{t}} s are {{t}}/{{tau}} time constants, so e^(−{{t}}/{{tau}}) of the step is still missing: the sensor reads {{a1}} °C.

decrement.title: Damping from two maxima
decrement.prompt: In a decay test one maximum reads {{first}} N·m and the next {{second}} N·m. What is the damping ratio D?
decrement.hint1: Take the logarithm of the ratio of two successive maxima: Λ = ln(xₙ/xₙ₊₁).
decrement.hint2: D = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²) — for a small Λ almost Λ/2π.
decrement.solution: Λ = ln({{first}}/{{second}}), and D = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²) = {{a1}}.

double_frequency.title: Twice the natural frequency
double_frequency.prompt: By what factor must the stiffness grow to multiply the natural frequency by {{factor}}, the inertia unchanged?
double_frequency.hint1: The natural frequency grows with the square root of the stiffness.
double_frequency.solution: f₀ grows with √c, so the stiffness has to grow by {{factor}}² = {{a1}}.

filter_delay.title: How late a filter makes a signal
filter_delay.prompt: A first-order filter with a corner at {{corner}} Hz carries a {{f}} Hz signal. How late does the signal arrive?
filter_delay.hint1: The phase of a first-order lag is −arctan(f/f_E).
filter_delay.hint2: A phase of φ degrees at a frequency f is a delay of φ/360° · 1/f.
filter_delay.solution: φ = −arctan({{f}}/{{corner}}), and at {{f}} Hz that is a delay of {{a1}} ms.

filter_phase.title: Phase and delay of a filter set too close
filter_phase.prompt: A first-order filter with a corner at {{corner}} Hz carries a {{f}} Hz signal. What is its phase, and what delay does that mean?
filter_phase.solution: φ = −arctan({{f}}/{{corner}}) = {{a1}}°, which at {{f}} Hz is a delay of {{a2}} ms — almost the filter's whole time constant.

euler_steps.title: Two Euler steps by hand
euler_steps.prompt: Euler with h = {{h}} s on the sensor with τ = {{tau}} s, stepped from {{start}} °C to {{final}} °C. What does it give after {{steps}} steps?
euler_steps.hint1: Each step adds h times the slope (y∞ − y)/τ taken at the start of the step.
euler_steps.hint2: The second step starts from the first step's result.
euler_steps.solution: Two steps of y ← y + h·(y∞ − y)/τ give {{a1}} °C — too high, because Euler holds the steepest slope, the one at the start of the step, for the whole step.

euler_gain.title: Euler on an undamped oscillator
euler_gain.prompt: Explicit Euler on an undamped oscillator with h·ω₀ = {{ratio}}: by what factor does the amplitude grow each step?
euler_gain.hint1: Euler multiplies each eigencomponent by 1 + hλ per step.
euler_gain.solution: |1 + j·{{ratio}}| = √(1 + {{ratio}}²) = {{a1}} per step: half a percent each step, more than a hundredfold in a thousand steps.

hand_estimate.title: The low mode by hand
hand_estimate.prompt: Estimate the two-mass rig's lowest natural frequency by hand: all its inertia ({{j1}} + {{j2}} kg·m²) on the two springs ({{c1}} and {{c2}} N·m/rad) in series.
hand_estimate.solution: c = {{c1}}·{{c2}}/({{c1}} + {{c2}}) N·m/rad on {{j1}} + {{j2}} kg·m² gives {{a1}} Hz. The exact mode is 6.94 Hz: the motor does not swing with the full amplitude, so less inertia takes part than the estimate assumes.

light_adapter.title: A lighter adapter
light_adapter.prompt: A lighter adapter, J₂ = {{j2}} kg·m², on the torsion bar c₂ = {{c2}} N·m/rad. By how much does the shaft misread at {{f}} Hz?
light_adapter.hint1: The shaft reads nothing at f_a = √(c₂/J₂)/2π.
light_adapter.solution: f_a = √({{c2}}/{{j2}})/2π, and (f/f_a)² = {{a1}} % — a lighter adapter moves f_a up and the error down.
